## GRETIL header

**Edition:** Durgaparasad and Kashinath Pandurang Parab, Bombay 1890, Kâvyamâlâ : a Collection of Old and Rare Sanskrit Kâvyas ... [= 'collective' Kavyamala series], Part VI, pp. 66-118.

**Entered by:** members of the Rasala team

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 879 CE – 1112 CE

**Posterior median:** 995 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu (Kashmir; Śaiva milieu, ethical/didactic)

**Genre:** kavya (didactic/satirical poem)

**Estimated date:** mid-11th c. CE (c. 1050)

A satirical and didactic poem in seven chapters (vicāras) totaling some 587 stanzas that attacks human pride (darpa). Each chapter targets a cause of arrogance—noble birth, wealth, learning, beauty, valor, charity, and asceticism—and illustrates through embedded narratives how such pride leads to ruin. The work moralizes against vanity and counsels humility.

**History:** Kṣemendra was an 11th-century Kashmiri polymath, satirist, and disciple of Abhinavagupta who wrote prolifically across genres. The Darpadalana belongs to his moralizing-satirical works (alongside the Kalāvilāsa and Deśopadeśa) and survives in the Kāvyamālā series; it is valued for its sharp social criticism of Kashmiri society.

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu (secular court poetry with grammatical/scientific purpose)

**Genre:** kavya / śāstra-kāvya (mahākāvya that illustrates grammar)

**Estimated date:** c. 6th-7th c. CE (often c. 600 CE)

A mahākāvya retelling the story of Rāma and the slaying of Rāvaṇa, paralleling the Rāmāyaṇa narrative across 22 cantos. Its distinguishing feature is that it systematically illustrates the rules of Pāṇinian grammar, poetic figures (alaṃkāra), and verbal moods, functioning simultaneously as poetry and as a teaching aid for Sanskrit grammar—the earliest exemplar of the 'instructional poem' (śāstra-kāvya).

**History:** The author is traditionally identified as Bhaṭṭi (sometimes equated with Bhartṛhari, though this is doubted); a colophon associates its composition with Valabhī under King Śrīdharasena. Its original title was Rāvaṇavadha, with Bhaṭṭikāvya being the later popular name. It became a standard pedagogical text and inspired later grammar-poems.

**Related works:** Rāmāyaṇa, Aṣṭādhyāyī

**Genre:** philosophical treatise (prakaraṇa)

**Estimated date:** c. 13th-14th c. CE (author c. 1269-1370)

A systematic Viśiṣṭādvaita treatise (also called Tarkasiddhāñjana) running to six chapters (paricchedas) that expounds the categories (padārtha) of reality—substance and attribute—within Rāmānuja's qualified non-dualism. It treats epistemology and ontology, presenting the world and all souls as constituting the 'body' of God (Brahman/Nārāyaṇa) of which he is the inner self.

**History:** Authored by Vedānta Deśika, the leading systematizer of post-Rāmānuja Śrīvaiṣṇava thought, it functions as a companion/continuation to his Nyāyapariśuddhi and is a foundational text of Viśiṣṭādvaita ontology, engaging and refuting Buddhist, Nyāya, and Advaita positions.

**Related works:** Nyāyapariśuddhi

**Tradition:** Hindu (theistic/Vedāntic; foundational across schools)

**Genre:** philosophical-religious poem (didactic episode within the epic)

**Estimated date:** c. 2nd c. BCE - 2nd c. CE

A 700-verse dialogue forming part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, in which the warrior Arjuna, despairing on the eve of the Kurukṣetra battle, is counseled by his charioteer Kṛṣṇa, revealed as the supreme deity. It synthesizes paths of disciplined action (karma-yoga), devotion (bhakti), and knowledge (jñāna), and includes Kṛṣṇa's theophany in chapter 11.

**History:** Embedded in the Mahābhārata but widely transmitted as an independent scripture, it became the most commented-upon Hindu text, with classic bhāṣyas by Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and Madhva, each reading it through their school. It is central to nearly all later Hindu theology and to the modern reception of Hinduism.

**Related works:** Mahābhārata, Mahābhārata: Bhīṣmaparvan

The great Sanskrit epic in eighteen books (parvans) of roughly 100,000 verses, narrating the dynastic struggle between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas culminating in the Kurukṣetra war. Beyond the central story it is an encyclopedic compendium of myth, genealogy, statecraft, and religious and philosophical teaching (including the Bhagavadgītā and the Śāntiparvan's dharma discourses), declaring 'what is here is found elsewhere; what is not here is nowhere.'

**History:** Traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa but universally recognized as a composite work that grew by accretion over several centuries; its text was reconstructed in the monumental Poona critical edition (Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1919-1966). It is foundational to Hindu civilization and has generated countless retellings and commentaries.

**Related works:** Harivaṃśa, Bhagavadgītā, Rāmāyaṇa

A collection of moral and political fables in mixed prose and verse, in which animal characters illustrate principles of practical wisdom (nīti), friendship, statecraft, war and peace. Structured as instruction given by a sage to ignorant princes, it is divided into four books: Mitralābha (acquiring friends), Suhṛdbheda (separating friends), Vigraha (war) and Sandhi (peace). It draws heavily on the Pañcatantra and other gnomic sources.

**History:** Attributed to Nārāyaṇa, who in the colophon credits a patron Dhaval(a)candra; it likely originated in eastern India under the Pāla dynasty. A vast philosophical work structured as Vasiṣṭha's instruction to the young prince Rāma, teaching liberation through the illusoriness of the world, the mind-made nature of reality, and the path of knowledge, illustrated by hundreds of intricate, often fantastical, frame-stories. **History:** Attributed to the poet Vālmīki, but the underlying text is the Kashmiri Mokṣopāya, composed (per Slaje and Hanneder) around the 10th century and subsequently reworked into an orthodox Advaita scripture with Trika overtones between the 11th and 14th centuries; the abridgment is credited to Abhinanda of Kashmir. It became a hugely popular text of practical non-dualist spirituality.

**Related works:** Mokṣopāya (Kashmiri urtext), Laghu-Yogavāsiṣṭha (Abhinanda), Rāmāyaṇa (framing association)

It became a central authority of the Bhāṭṭa school and exerted wide influence on later Mīmāṃsā, Dharmaśāstra exegesis, and the broader debate with Buddhism. It systematizes non-dual Śaiva metaphysics, the means to liberation (the upāyas), initiation, ritual, mantra, the divine energies, and the sacred calendar, interpreting tantric practice through the philosophical categories of the Pratyabhijñā. Utpaladeva's own concise commentary (vṛtti) on his Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, the verse foundation of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') philosophy. The work argues that liberation comes through the recognition that one's own self is identical with the supreme Lord (Śiva), grounding a monistic, idealist, and theistic system in a sophisticated theory of consciousness, agency, and cognition.

**History:** Composed by Utpaladeva, pupil of Somānanda (the school's founder), around 925 CE; Abhinavagupta reports that the kārikās and the vṛtti were written together. The kārikās with this vṛtti became the doctrinal core of the Pratyabhijñā, later expounded in Abhinavagupta's two large commentaries (the Vimarśinī and the Vivṛtivimarśinī). It is the pivotal philosophical text of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism.

The earliest surviving systematic text of the Sāṃkhya school, consisting of roughly 72 verses in the ārya metre (hence the alternative title Sāṃkhyasaptati, 'the seventy [verses] of Sāṃkhya'). The work became the foundational text of classical Sāṃkhya and attracted numerous commentaries, including the Yuktidīpikā, Gauḍapāda's bhāṣya, Vācaspati Miśra's Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī, and the Sāṃkhyavṛtti; a Chinese translation by Paramārtha (6th c.) helps fix its date.

Across four chapters it interprets the terse aphorisms to argue that Brahman is the sole non-dual reality, that the individual self (ātman) is identical with Brahman, that the empirical world is grounded in māyā/avidyā, and it refutes rival schools (Sāṃkhya, Nyāya, Buddhism, etc.).

It generated a vast subcommentarial literature, most notably Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī and Padmapāda's Pañcapādikā, which gave rise to the two main Advaita exegetical schools (Bhāmatī and Vivaraṇa).

The 'Veda of melodies/chants,' the third Veda, consisting largely of verses (mostly drawn from the Ṛgveda) arranged and set to melodies (sāman) for liturgical singing by the udgātṛ priests during the soma sacrifice. The oldest of the four Vedas and one of the oldest extant texts in any Indo-European language, comprising 1,028 hymns (sūktas) in ten books (maṇḍalas) addressed mainly to deities such as Indra, Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, and the Aśvins. Alongside ritual invocations it contains cosmogonic, philosophical, and gnomic hymns (e.g. the Puruṣasūkta and the Nāsadīya 'Creation Hymn'). This record ('rvh') corresponds to a metrically restored/Holland-Van Nooten-style edition.

**History:** Composed and transmitted orally with extraordinary fidelity over millennia, the Ṛgveda is the cultural and religious bedrock of the Indian tradition and a primary source for Indo-Aryan history and Proto-Indo-European studies. Its family books (II-VII) are the oldest stratum, with books I and X added later.

**Related works:** Sāmaveda-Saṃhitā, Aitareya-Brāhmaṇa, Kauṣītaki-Brāhmaṇa, Āśvalāyana- and Śāṅkhāyana-Gṛhyasūtras

The 'Black' Yajurveda is one of the two main recensions of the Yajurveda, the Veda of sacrificial formulas (yajus) used by the adhvaryu priest in the performance of Vedic ritual. Distinctively, the Kṛṣṇa ('black') recension intermixes mantra (verse formulas) with prose Brahmana-style ritual exegesis directly within the saṃhitā, in contrast to the 'White' (Śukla) Yajurveda which separates them. Its surviving schools include the Taittirīya, Maitrāyaṇī, Kāṭhaka and Kapiṣṭhala saṃhitās.

**History:** Transmitted orally with extraordinary fidelity through priestly schools (śākhā), the Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda predates and conditioned the development of the later Vedic ritual and Brahmana literature. The label 'black/unarranged' versus the 'white/well-arranged' Śukla recension reflects a traditional account (Yājñavalkya's separation) of the differing organization of mantra and explanatory prose.

**Related works:** Yajurveda, Śukla-Yajurveda, Taittirīya-Saṃhitā, Maitrāyaṇī-Saṃhitā, Kāṭhaka-Saṃhitā

A prātiśākhya is a treatise on the phonetics, sandhi (euphonic combination), accent, and correct recitation peculiar to a particular Vedic school (śākhā). The Taittirīya-Prātiśākhya governs the recitation of the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, specifying how the continuous (saṃhitā) text relates to its word-by-word (pada) analysis. It is a key early document of Indian phonetic science (śikṣā).

**History:** The prātiśākhyas are among the oldest extant works of systematic Indian linguistic analysis, predating or paralleling the formal grammar of Pāṇini, and they preserve precise descriptions of articulation that helped guarantee accurate oral transmission of the Veda. The Taittirīya-Prātiśākhya is attached specifically to the Taittirīya school.

**Related works:** Taittirīya-Saṃhitā, Kṛṣṇa-Yajurveda, Ṛk-Prātiśākhya, Vājasaneyi-Prātiśākhya

The 'Heart Sūtra' is the most concise and most famous of the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā) texts. In a dialogue framed around Avalokiteśvara addressing Śāriputra, it distills the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā): that the five aggregates are empty, encapsulated in the formula 'form is emptiness, emptiness is form,' and culminating in the mantra 'gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.'

**History:** Among the most influential and widely recited Buddhist texts in East Asian and Tibetan traditions, it exists in shorter and longer recensions. 'The Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla,' an early Mahāyāna sūtra included in the Ratnakūṭa collection, in which the bodhisattva Rāṣṭrapāla questions the Buddha about the bodhisattva path. It exalts the rigorous forest-dwelling, ascetic bodhisattva ideal and sharply criticizes lax, worldly monks, framing the decline of the Dharma as a result of monastic corruption.

The Lalitavistara, 'The Play in Full' (the 'extensive account of the sport/display' of the Buddha), is an elaborate, semi-legendary biography of Śākyamuni from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven through his birth, youth, renunciation, awakening under the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of the Dharma at Sārnāth. It presents the Buddha's life as the deliberate, miraculous display (lalita) of an already-awakened being.

**History:** A composite work showing a Mahāyāna reworking of older Sarvāstivāda biographical traditions, it was translated into Chinese and Tibetan and was hugely influential on Buddhist art, notably the narrative reliefs of Borobudur. Its dating is layered; portions are early while the received Sanskrit text reflects later redaction.

**Related works:** Buddhacarita (Aśvaghoṣa), Mahāvastu, Sarvāstivāda Vinaya biographical material

The 'Rice Seedling Sūtra' takes as its image a stalk of rice growing from a seed to illustrate and expound the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). A modern Sanskrit translation of the Christian Bible, produced by Protestant missionaries to render the scriptures into the classical learned language of India. It comprises the New Testament and Old Testament rendered into Sanskrit, adapting biblical prose and concepts into Sanskrit idiom.

The sixth book, the 'Book of War' (also called Laṅkākāṇḍa). It narrates the building of the bridge (setu) to Laṅkā, the great battle between Rāma's monkey army and Rāvaṇa's demons, the deaths of Kumbhakarṇa, Indrajit, and finally Rāvaṇa, the rescue of Sītā and her trial by fire (agniparīkṣā), and the triumphal return to Ayodhyā for Rāma's coronation.

**History:** The climactic and longest action book of the epic's ancient core, it brings the central narrative to its resolution. In most recensions the original story effectively concludes here, with the Uttarakāṇḍa regarded as a later appendix.

The seventh and final book, the 'Later Book.' It recounts events after Rāma's coronation: the history and genealogy of Rāvaṇa and the rākṣasas, Hanumān's origins, and—most famously—Rāma's banishment of the pregnant Sītā in response to public doubt of her chastity. **History:** The Uttarakāṇḍa is, with the Bālakāṇḍa, the part of the Rāmāyaṇa most consistently judged by scholars to be a later interpolation, on grounds of its more explicit divinization of Rāma, narrative inconsistencies, and absence from the oldest manuscripts. Its treatment of Sītā's exile has been a major focus of later literary, devotional, and critical engagement.

**Tradition:** Hindu; Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), Kashmiri

**Genre:** philosophical/literary treatise on poetics (kārikā + vṛtti)

**Estimated date:** c. mid-to-late 9th c. CE (Ānandavardhana fl. c. 820-890 CE, Kashmir)

The first chapter (uddyota) of the Dhvanyāloka ('Light on Suggestion'), the foundational work of the dhvani school of Sanskrit poetics. It introduces and defends the thesis that dhvani—suggested or implied meaning—is the very soul (ātman) of poetry, distinguishing the literal/denoted sense from the more powerful suggested sense, against rival theorists who deny suggestion's existence.

**History:** Ānandavardhana, a court scholar under King Avantivarman of Kashmir, established dhvani as the dominant theory of Indian aesthetics. A debate (going back to Abhinavagupta) holds that the kārikās may be by an earlier 'Dhvanikāra' (called Sahṛdaya, hence the alternate title Sahṛdayāloka) while Ānandavardhana wrote the prose vṛtti; others ascribe the whole to him. Abhinavagupta's commentary, the Locana, became its classic exposition.

**Related works:** Dhvanyāloka, Locana (Abhinavagupta), Kāvyaprakāśa

The second chapter of the Dhvanyāloka. It develops a typology of suggestion, treating in particular the relation of dhvani to rasa (aesthetic emotion), the varieties of suggested meaning, and the way figures of speech (alaṃkāras), qualities (guṇas), and rasa-dhvani operate. It elaborates the famous doctrine that the suggestion of rasa is the highest kind of dhvani.

**History:** Part of Ānandavardhana's four-uddyota treatise that reoriented Sanskrit poetics around suggestion and made rasa-dhvani its central category, profoundly influencing Abhinavagupta, Mammaṭa, and the whole later tradition.

The third and longest chapter of the Dhvanyāloka. It analyzes suggestion in fine grain, distinguishing the suggestion of bare matter, of figures, and of rasa; it discusses how the suggested meaning is conveyed by the power of words and sense, the relation between principal and subordinate suggestion (guṇībhūta-vyaṅgya), and the proper deployment of figures, qualities, and styles in service of rasa.

**History:** This chapter contains much of the technical machinery of dhvani theory and its applications to literary composition, and was extensively commented upon by Abhinavagupta in his Locana.

**Related works:** Dhvanyāloka, Locana (Abhinavagupta), Kāvyaprakāśa

The fourth and concluding chapter of the Dhvanyāloka. **History:** The final uddyota rounds off Ānandavardhana's argument by celebrating the boundless expressive potential of poetry grounded in suggestion, securing the Dhvanyāloka's status as the cornerstone of classical Indian literary theory.

The foundational treatise of the dhvani ('suggestion/resonance') school of Sanskrit literary theory. It argues that the soul of poetry (kāvya) is not its literal sense or its ornaments but the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha), realized especially as suggested aesthetic mood (rasa-dhvani). Whether the kārikās and vṛtti are by one or two hands has been debated.

One of the earliest extant systematic treatises on Sanskrit poetics, in six chapters (paricchedas) totaling about 398 verses. It treats the nature and aims of poetry, poetic faults (doṣa), figures of speech (alaṃkāra), and correctness of language, and is foundational to the alaṃkāra ('ornament') school. A popular, elementary verse handbook of Sanskrit poetics in ten chapters (mayūkhas), totaling about 350 verses. A major treatise arguing that the essence ('life', jīvita) of all literature is vakrokti, 'oblique/striking expression'—the creative deviation of poetic language from ordinary usage. Kuntaka develops an elaborate six-fold typology of vakratā ('crookedness/strikingness') ranging from the level of phonemes and words up to whole works, presenting it as a unifying principle of poetic beauty.

**History:** Kuntaka, a Kashmiri theorist usually dated between Ānandavardhana (9th c.) and Abhinavagupta (10th-11th c.), reworked Bhāmaha's notion of vakrokti into a comprehensive aesthetic. The text survives incompletely; it was critically edited by S. K. De (1923/1928). It represents an alternative to the dominant dhvani school.

**Related works:** Kāvyālaṃkāra (Bhāmaha), Dhvanyāloka (Ānandavardhana)

## GRETIL header

**Edition:** Ganganatha Jha: Kāvyaprakāśa of Mammaṭa, with English translation, rev. ed., Varanasi : Bharatiya Vidya Prakaśan, 1967 (2 parts). With occasional corrections according to the ed. by N.S. Venkatanathacharya: The Kavyaprakasha of Mammata, with Sanketa of Acharya Manikyachandra, Madhumati of Ravi Bhattacharya and Bhavukapriya tippani, Mysore : Oriental Research Institute, 1974 (2 vols).

**Entered by:** Masahiro Takano

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 1025 CE – 1123 CE

**Posterior median:** 1074 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu; Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), Kashmiri

**Genre:** philosophical treatise on poetics (kārikā with vṛtti)

**Estimated date:** c. late 11th-early 12th c. CE

The single most influential and widely taught compendium of Sanskrit poetics, in ten chapters (ullāsas) of verse kārikās with prose explanation and illustrative examples. It synthesizes the dhvani (suggestion) and alaṃkāra (ornament) traditions, treating the nature and purpose of poetry, word-functions (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, vyañjanā), faults, qualities, figures, and the classification of poetry by suggestion.

**History:** By Mammaṭa, a Kashmiri scholar of the late 11th-12th c.; the final portion is traditionally said to have been completed by a second hand (Allaṭa/Alaka). It became the standard textbook of poetics, attracting over fifty commentaries—reputedly second only to the Bhagavadgītā among Sanskrit works in number of commentaries.

**Related works:** Dhvanyāloka (Ānandavardhana), Locana (Abhinavagupta)

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu; Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), Kashmiri

**Genre:** philosophical treatise (short monograph on semantics/poetics)

**Estimated date:** c. late 11th-early 12th c. CE

A short specialized treatise ('Inquiry into the Operations of the Word') by Mammaṭa setting out the semantic functions of language—denotation (abhidhā), indication (lakṣaṇā), and suggestion (vyañjanā)—and defending the independence of vyañjanā as the basis of poetic suggestion. It argues against critics (notably Mukula Bhaṭṭa) who tried to reduce suggestion to the other functions.

**History:** A lesser-known companion piece to Mammaṭa's Kāvyaprakāśa, concentrating on the theory of word-power that underlies the dhvani doctrine. It is an important source for the Sanskrit philosophy of language as applied to poetics.

**Related works:** Kāvyaprakāśa (Mammaṭa), Abhidhāvṛttimātṛkā (Mukula Bhaṭṭa)

**Tradition:** Hindu; Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra)

**Genre:** philosophical treatise on poetics (practical handbook, partly in sūtra style)

**Estimated date:** c. 880-920 CE (late 9th-early 10th c.)

A practical handbook (originally planned in eighteen sections, of which the first, the Kavirahasya, survives) on the making of a poet. It discusses the poet's training, talent (pratibhā) and learning, the literary 'assembly', plagiarism, regional styles, and the geography and conventions (kavi-samaya) of poetic composition rather than abstract aesthetics.

**History:** By Rājaśekhara, a poet-dramatist and court scholar of the Pratihāra kings Mahendrapāla and Mahīpāla. The Kāvyamīmāṃsā is unusual in its sociological and pedagogical orientation and is a valuable source on the poetic culture and literary geography of early medieval India.

**Related works:** Karpūramañjarī (Rājaśekhara), Kāvyaprakāśa (Mammaṭa)

**Genre:** treatise on dramaturgy

**Estimated date:** c. mid-16th c. CE

A treatise ('Moonlight of Drama') on the rules of dramaturgy, summarizing classical Sanskrit nāṭya theory (dramatic types, plot structure, sentiments) and adapting it to Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional drama. It provides the technical framework underlying Rūpa's own devotional plays on Kṛṣṇa.

**History:** By Rūpa Gosvāmī (c. 1489-1564), one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana and a leading theologian of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava movement founded by Caitanya. The work supports his project of recasting classical rasa-dramaturgy in the service of bhakti, as realized in his plays Vidagdha-mādhava and Lalita-mādhava.

**Related works:** Nāṭyaśāstra (Bharata), Vidagdha-mādhava (Rūpa Gosvāmī), Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu (Rūpa Gosvāmī)

**Tradition:** Hindu; Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), Kashmiri

**Genre:** bhasya/commentary (vyākhyā on a poetics treatise)

**Estimated date:** c. 1125-1150 CE (12th c.)

A commentary by Ruyyaka on Mahima Bhaṭṭa's Vyaktiviveka. The base text (Vyaktiviveka) argues against the dhvani theory, holding that what others call 'suggestion' is really a form of inference (anumāna), so that rasa is inferred rather than directly manifested; Ruyyaka's vyākhyā systematically expounds and evaluates these positions.

**History:** Ruyyaka, a 12th-century Kashmiri theorist and teacher (reputedly of Maṅkha), was among the first to reflect systematically on Mahima Bhaṭṭa's notion of vyakti ('manifestation'). The commentary is an important witness to the debate between the dhvani school (Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta) and its critics.

**Related works:** Vyaktiviveka (Mahima Bhaṭṭa), Dhvanyāloka (Ānandavardhana)

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu; Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), Kashmiri

**Genre:** philosophical treatise on poetics (sūtra/kārikā with author's vṛtti)

**Estimated date:** c. mid-12th c. CE (c. 1135-1150)

A systematic treatise ('The Whole Treasury of Ornament') devoted chiefly to the classification and analysis of figures of speech (alaṃkāra). Ruyyaka treats roughly eighty-two figures—a small number of word-figures (śabdālaṃkāra) and the majority sense-figures (arthālaṃkāra)—defining and exemplifying each within a dhvani-informed framework.

**History:** By Rājānaka Ruyyaka, a 12th-century Kashmiri scholar writing some two and a half centuries after Ānandavardhana. The work became a standard reference on figures and is best known together with the elaborate commentary (Vimarśinī) of Jayaratha. (Authorship has occasionally been linked to Maṅkha, Ruyyaka's pupil.)

**Related works:** Vimarśinī (Jayaratha, commentary), Kāvyaprakāśa (Mammaṭa), Dhvanyāloka (Ānandavardhana)

**Estimated date:** c. early-to-mid 14th c. CE (fl. c. 1330)

A treatise ('Moon to the Ocean of Aesthetic Sentiment'), arranged in three 'rays' (vilāsas), giving an exhaustive account of rasa theory—the sentiments, their determinants and consequents, the hero and heroine typology (nāyaka-nāyikā-bheda), states of love, and dramatic conventions. It draws heavily on the Nāṭyaśāstra and Daśarūpaka traditions and is widely cited by later writers.

**History:** By Siṃhabhūpāla, a king of the Recherla (Velama) line in Andhra, a learned patron also credited with the music treatise Saṅgītasudhākara, active around 1330. His work on rasa is quoted by the commentator Mallinātha, attesting its early authority. Critically edited by T. Venkatacharya (Adyar Library, 1979).

**Related works:** Nāṭyaśāstra (Bharata), Daśarūpaka (Dhanañjaya), Saṅgītasudhākara (Siṃhabhūpāla)

A concise compendium ('Collection of the Essence of the Ornaments of Poetry') treating about forty-one figures of speech (alaṃkāras), word- and sense-based, organized in six groups, each defined and illustrated. The encyclopedic foundational treatise on the performing arts, traditionally in 36 chapters. A short Sanskrit devotional hymn, also called Mohamudgara ('hammer that destroys delusion'), urging the listener to worship Govinda (Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu) and abandon attachment to worldly wealth, pride in scholarship, and sensual desire in light of the inevitability of death. **History:** Traditionally ascribed to Ādi Śaṅkara, said to have been improvised in Varanasi on seeing an old man memorizing grammar; the so-called Dvādaśamañjarikā core is attributed to Śaṅkara with additional verses attributed to his disciples (Caturdaśamañjarikā), yielding a transmitted text of around 31-33 verses. It is one of the most popular short devotional poems in the Advaita tradition, frequently set to music and commented upon.

**Related works:** Mohamudgara, Vivekacūḍāmaṇi

The Gāhākoṣa (Sanskrit Gāthākośa/Gāthāsaptaśatī, 'Treasury of Verses' or 'Seven Hundred Verses') is an anthology of roughly seven hundred single-stanza lyric poems (gāthās) in Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit, mostly in the Āryā metre, traditionally attributed to or compiled by the Sātavāhana king Hāla. The verses, drawn from many poets, vividly evoke rural Deccan life, nature, and erotic love, frequently voiced from a woman's perspective with suggestive, allusive imagery.

**History:** The oldest surviving Prakrit lyric anthology, its core is dated to the early centuries CE, though the collection grew through later recensions and accreted commentaries; the project metadata's 1200-1300 CE hint is incorrect for the work's composition. It deeply influenced later Sanskrit erotic muktaka poetry, including Govardhana's Āryāsaptaśatī, which was modeled on it.

**Related works:** Āryāsaptaśatī (Govardhana), Amaruśataka

A lyric poem in the mandākrāntā metre in which an exiled yakṣa, separated from his beloved, asks a passing rain cloud to carry a message of love to her in the Himalayan city of Alakā. The poem's first half (Pūrvamegha) maps the cloud's route across northern India, while the second half (Uttaramegha) describes Alakā and the lovesick wife. The Bhāratamañjarī is Kṣemendra's verse condensation of the entire Mahābhārata, rendering Vyāsa's epic into a compact poetic summary in his own words. This section corresponds to the nineteenth book, the Harivaṃśa, the genealogical and Krishna-centred appendix (khila) of the Mahābhārata that narrates the lineage of Hari (Vishnu/Krishna), the creation, and the deeds of Krishna. Kṣemendra preserves the narrative substance while upholding śānta (serenity) as the work's predominant rasa.

**History:** Kṣemendra (c. 990–1070 CE) was a prolific Kashmiri polymath who studied under Abhinavagupta and Vaishnava teachers; he was renowned as a master 'abridger' (mañjarī-maker) who also condensed the Rāmāyaṇa (Rāmāyaṇamañjarī) and Guṇāḍhya's Bṛhatkathā. The Bhāratamañjarī is an important witness to the form of the Mahābhārata circulating in 11th-century Kashmir.

The actual date and authorship are unknown and the work is far later than the legendary attribution. Identification of this specific 'Śivastuti' with the Śiva Tāṇḍava Stotra is probable but not certain.

The Śiśupālavadha ('The Slaying of Śiśupāla') is a mahākāvya in 20 cantos that elaborates an episode from the Mahābhārata: Krishna's killing of the insolent king Śiśupāla of Chedi at Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice. The narrative serves as a frame for dazzling poetic ornamentation, learned description, and metrical and verbal virtuosity rather than for plot alone.

**History:** Composed by Māgha (son of Dattaka), probably in the late 7th or early 8th century in western India (Śrīmāla/Bhinmal). It is counted among the five canonical mahākāvyas and gave rise to the proverb 'in Māgha are found the three—simile, words, and meaning' (the poet who rivals Kālidāsa and Bhāravi). It is famous for citra (constrained/figured verse) display.

The Setubandha ('Building of the Bridge'), also called Rāvaṇavaho ('The Slaying of Rāvaṇa'), is a mahākāvya composed in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit that narrates the Rāmāyaṇa episode of Rāma's army building the bridge (setu) to Lanka and the ensuing war against Rāvaṇa. It is celebrated for its elaborate descriptive set-pieces and is the principal surviving early Prakrit court epic.

**History:** It is attributed to a king Pravarasena (commonly identified with the Vākāṭaka ruler Pravarasena II); tradition variously connects it to Kālidāsa as well. Dating is disputed between the mid-3rd and the 5th century CE. It is the earliest extant Prakrit mahākāvya and was hugely influential as a model of Prakrit poetic style.

**Related works:** Rāmāyaṇa

The Śṛṅgāratilaka ('Ornament of the Erotic') is a short treatise on Sanskrit poetics devoted specifically to rasa (aesthetic emotion), and especially to śṛṅgāra, the erotic sentiment. It is notable as the first independent Indian work to take rasa—and the typology of lovers (nāyaka/nāyikā) and the erotic mood—as its sole subject, illustrating the theory with verses.

The work is an important early link in the history of rasa theory and of nāyikābheda (classification of heroines). Sheldon Pollock has worked on a critical edition/translation.

The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Nāgas') is a five-act play that dramatizes the legend of the vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana, who, embodying Buddhist compassion, offers his own body to the bird-god Garuḍa to save a young Nāga destined to be devoured, thereby ending Garuḍa's slaughter of the serpents. It blends a romantic first portion (Jīmūtavāhana's love for Malayavatī) with a strongly self-sacrificial, Bodhisattva-like climax.

**History:** Attributed to the emperor Harṣa of Kanauj (also credited with the plays Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā). The Nāgānanda is unusual for its Buddhist ethos and its benedictory verse to the Buddha (and/or Gaurī), reflecting Harṣa's syncretic patronage. The story parallels material later found in the Kathāsaritsāgara.

**Related works:** Ratnāvalī, Priyadarśikā, Bṛhatkathā / Kathāsaritsāgara

A four-act romantic court comedy (nāṭikā) recounting the love affair between King Udayana of Vatsa and Ratnāvalī (Sāgarikā), a Ceylonese princess who, shipwrecked, enters the court of Udayana's chief queen Vāsavadattā as a maidservant. **History:** Conventionally attributed to the emperor Harṣa of Kanauj, though some scholars argue a court poet (sometimes named Dhāvaka or Bāṇa) composed the dramas issued under his name. The play is a model of the nāṭikā subgenre and is celebrated for its refined handling of the love-intrigue plot derived ultimately from the Bṛhatkathā tradition.

**Related works:** Priyadarśikā, Nāgānanda, Harṣacarita, Bṛhatkathā

A one-act Sanskrit farce (prahasana) set in Kāñcīpuram, the Pallava capital. A seven-act political drama dramatizing the statecraft of Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya) as he maneuvers to win over Rākṣasa, the loyal minister of the overthrown Nanda dynasty, to the service of the new Mauryan emperor Candragupta. Unusually for Sanskrit drama, it contains no romantic plot and centers entirely on espionage, forged seals (mudrā), and diplomatic intrigue.

**History:** By the poet Viśākhadatta, about whose life little is known; his dating is debated over several centuries. The play is prized as a masterwork of plot construction and as a literary window onto ancient Indian political theory, drawing on the Arthaśāstra tradition.

**Related works:** Arthaśāstra, Devīcandragupta

The "second" Rājataraṅginī, a Sanskrit verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir continuing Kalhaṇa's original from c. 1148/1149 CE down to the reign of Sultan Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (mid-15th c.). It documents in detail the transition to the Kashmir Sultanate and the Islamization of the valley, with Jonarāja writing in part as an eyewitness.

**History:** Composed by the Kashmirian poet-historian Jonarāja (died 1459), court historian to Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn. One textual recension incorporates roughly 350 additional verses interpolated in the later 16th century by an anonymous continuator known as "Pseudo-Jonarāja." The chronicle was itself continued by Jonarāja's pupil Śrīvara.

**Related works:** Rājataraṅginī (Kalhaṇa), Jaina-Rājataraṅginī (Śrīvara)

A regional Purāṇa of Kashmir presented as the sage Bṛhadaśva's instruction to King Janamejaya on the origins and sacred order of the Kashmir valley. It recounts the draining of the primeval lake by Viṣṇu and the establishment of the Nāga Nīla's worship, and prescribes the valley's tīrthas (pilgrimage sites), festivals, and ritual calendar, incorporating indigenous Nāga and Piśāca traditions.

**History:** The Nīlamata is the principal early source for the religious geography and customs of Kashmir, drawn on heavily by Kalhaṇa in the 12th-century Rājataraṅgiṇī. Scholars (e.g. Ved Kumari Ghai) date its core to roughly the 6th-8th century CE, with later interpolations; it was edited and translated in modern times by Ved Kumari Ghai.

**Related works:** Rājataraṅgiṇī, Mahābhārata

A Jain philosophical work of some 700 verses surveying, examining, and critically engaging the doctrines of the major non-Jain schools and sects — including Buddhist, Sāṃkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, materialist, and theistic positions — refuting and reconciling them while upholding the Jain (anekānta) standpoint, treated with notable respect toward opponents. It is a key Jain doxographical and inclusivist text.

**Related works:** Yogadṛṣṭisamuccaya, Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya

An 'Investigation into the True Teaching,' a Digambara Jain philosophical work that presents and refutes twelve rival Indian philosophical systems — including Puruṣādvaita (Advaita Vedānta), Śabdādvaita (grammarians), Vijñānādvaita (Yogācāra), Citrādvaita, Cārvāka, Sautrāntika Buddhism, theistic and non-theistic Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, and Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā — in order to establish Jainism as the sole 'true teaching.'

**History:** Composed by the Digambara logician Vidyānandin (Vidyānanda), generally placed in the 9th-10th c. CE. Known since around 1920 but long understudied, it was first edited by Gokul Chandra Jain (1964); Jens W. Borgland produced a critical edition and study (Harrassowitz, 2020). It is an important source for late first-millennium inter-school polemic.

**Related works:** Āptaparīkṣā, Pramāṇaparīkṣā, Tattvārthaślokavārttika

**Estimated date:** c. 12th-13th c. CE (recension/version one)

A foundational haṭha-yoga manual of the Nātha tradition, the 'Hundred Verses of Gorakṣa,' which outlines yogic limbs including āsana, prāṇāyāma, mudrā, the cakras and the raising of kuṇḍalinī (notably the technique of 'stimulating Sarasvatī'). Though ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, the surviving texts postdate the historical figure.

**Related works:** Vivekamārtaṇḍa, Gorakṣasaṃhitā, Haṭhapradīpikā, Amaraugha

A celebrated Tantric devotional hymn of c. 100 verses in the śikhariṇī metre praising the Goddess Tripurasundarī (Lalitā). The first portion (the Ānandalaharī, c. 41 verses) expounds the worship of the Śrīcakra and the union of Śiva-Śakti, while the remainder offers an extended head-to-foot (keśādipāda) aesthetic description of the Goddess's beauty.

It has attracted dozens of commentaries (notably Lakṣmīdhara's) and remains one of the most popular and most-recited Śākta hymns.

**Related works:** Lalitāsahasranāma, Tripurasundarī Śrīvidyā corpus, Ānandalaharī

**Genre:** philosophical treatise

**Estimated date:** c. 900-925 CE

Chapters 1-3 of the Śivadṛṣṭi ('Vision of Śiva'), the foundational philosophical work of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') school of Kashmir Shaivism. The text argues a strict non-dualism in which all beings and things in the universe are fully identical with the active, willful god Śiva, the conscious world being real rather than illusory; the opening chapters set out this Śiva-as-everything pantheism and its theory of will (icchā) and divine power (śakti).

**History:** Somānanda was the first systematic philosopher of the Trika/Pratyabhijñā lineage and teacher of Utpaladeva, who developed his ideas in the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā. The Śivadṛṣṭi is regarded as the first full scholastic philosophical treatise of the school; it survives with the commentary (vṛtti) of Utpaladeva.

**Related works:** Śivadṛṣṭi (complete), Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti (Utpaladeva)

Also called the Aṣṭāvakra Saṃhitā, a verse dialogue between the sage Aṣṭāvakra and King Janaka expounding radical non-dualism (Advaita): the self is pure, free, witnessing consciousness, and liberation is recognition of one's ever-already-free nature rather than the fruit of any practice. It is admired for its uncompromising, terse statement of jñāna.

**History:** Authorship and date are highly uncertain and much disputed: estimates range from c. 500-400 BCE (Mukerjee) to the 8th or 14th century CE (Brockington), the later dating favored because of its developed, systematic Advaita. It is attributed to the legendary sage Aṣṭāvakra known from the Mahābhārata and Purāṇas.

**Related works:** Bhagavadgītā, Advaita Vedānta corpus

A Sanskrit devotional hymn of about 40 verses addressed to Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu as Mukunda, the bestower of liberation. The verses express ardent surrender (prapatti) and longing for the Lord, including the famous prayer to remember Kṛṣṇa at the moment of death, and extol single-minded devotion over even liberation.

**History:** Attributed to Kulaśekhara, the poet-saint counted among the twelve Āḻvārs of the Tamil Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition, identified with a Cera (Kulaśekhara) ruler of Kerala; the hymn is traditionally associated with the Raṅganātha temple at Śrīraṅgam. Its authorship and date are debated, but it is a celebrated and widely commented Vaiṣṇava stotra. The project hint of c. 900–1099 CE is broadly consistent with common datings.

The foundational systematic treatise on bhakti-rasa, adapting the classical rasa theory of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra into a theology of devotion. **Genre:** philosophical treatise (sandarbha)

**Estimated date:** c. late 16th c. CE

The third of the six Sandarbhas, examining the nature of the individual self (jīva), the operation of māyā, and the immanent presence of the Absolute as Paramātmā (the Supersoul) pervading and sustaining the cosmos and all beings. It elaborates the relation between the soul, the material energy, and the indwelling Lord.

**History:** Continuing Jīva Gosvāmī's systematic Bhāgavata Vedānta, it treats the theme of sambandha alongside the Tattva- and Bhāgavata-sandarbhas, working out the metaphysics of jīva and māyā that underpins the school's acintya-bhedābheda (inconceivable difference-and-non-difference) doctrine.

**Related works:** Ṣaṭsandarbha, Bhāgavatasandarbha, Kṛṣṇasandarbha, Bhāgavata Purāṇa

**Genre:** philosophical-theological treatise (with commentary on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa)

**Estimated date:** mid-16th c. CE (c. 1555-1561)

The fourth of Jīva Gosvāmī's six Sandarbhas (Ṣaṭsandarbha or Bhāgavata-sandarbha), a systematic exposition of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology drawing heavily on the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. The Kṛṣṇasandarbha argues that Kṛṣṇa, not a mere avatāra, is the original and complete form of Bhagavān (svayaṃ bhagavān), and establishes him as the supreme object of loving devotion, treating his līlā, dhāman (Vraja), and associates.

**History:** Jīva Gosvāmī (c. 1513-1598), nephew of Rūpa and Sanātana Gosvāmī, systematized the theology of the Caitanya movement at Vrindavan; the Sandarbhas were partly based on notes of Gopāla Bhaṭṭa. They remain the doctrinal foundation of the Gauḍīya school and were commented upon by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

**Related works:** Ṣaṭsandarbha (Bhāgavata-sandarbha), Bhāgavata Purāṇa, Tattvasandarbha, Bhagavatsandarbha, Paramātmasandarbha

The fifth of the Ṣaṭsandarbhas, devoted to bhakti (devotion). **Estimated date:** mid-16th c. CE (c. 1555-1561)

The sixth and final Sandarbha, treating prīti or prema-bhakti — pure love of God — as the supreme goal (prayojana) of human life. It analyzes the nature of divine love, its relation to liberation (which it surpasses), the rasa-theology of devotional emotion, and the eternal blissful relationship between the soul and Kṛṣṇa.

**History:** The culminating volume of Jīva Gosvāmī's Ṣaṭsandarbha, completing the structure of sambandha (relation), abhidheya (means) and prayojana (goal). It is foundational for Gauḍīya aesthetics of devotion and was commented upon by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

**Estimated date:** c. 925-950 CE (first half of 10th c.)

A short philosophical work ('Proof of a Sentient/Non-inert Knower'), one of the three treatises of Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī. It argues for the necessity of a conscious, self-luminous knowing subject, against Buddhist and other positions that would reduce cognition to insentient processes, and shows that the limited individual knower is ultimately grounded in the one unlimited Self, establishing the non-dual nature of reality.

**History:** Utpaladeva (c. 900-950 CE) was the chief originator of the Pratyabhijñā ('recognition') system of monistic Kashmir Śaivism, building on his teacher Somānanda and later developed by Abhinavagupta. The Siddhitrayī (Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi, Īśvarasiddhi, Sambandhasiddhi) accompanies his major work the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā; the text survives with a Vṛtti.

The mantra-portion ('Mantrapraśna', in praśnas) of the Vaikhānasa corpus, containing the liturgical mantras used in Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava temple and domestic worship. It includes numerous accented mantras of clearly Vedic character not found in other Yajurveda Saṃhitās, supplying formulae for the consecration and worship of Viṣṇu and associated deities.

**History:** The Vaikhānasas, followers of the sage Vikhanas, are the hereditary priests (arcakas) of more than half the Viṣṇu temples of South India, including Tirupati. Their tradition claims direct Vedic descent and is regarded as more orthodox/conservative than the Pāñcarātra. The Mantrapraśna is the mantra core complementing the Vaikhānasa Gṛhya/Smārta sūtras and Āgama saṃhitās; a critical edition/translation of Mantrapraśna V-VIII was published by Harvard University Press.

**Related works:** Vaikhānasa Gṛhyasūtra, Vaikhānasa Āgama / saṃhitās, Taittirīya Saṃhitā

**History:** Studied by R. C. It is to be distinguished from the encyclopedic Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa, of which it is the conceptual predecessor; a critical edition was prepared by R. Grünendahl.

A Pāñcarātra Āgama scripture of roughly 2800 verses in 39 chapters, dealing with image-worship and temple ritual: the theology and consecration of pratimā icons, iconographic prescriptions, and the construction of the prāsāda (temple structure) to house the images. Its precise date and authorship are unknown, as is typical of the Pāñcarātra revelatory literature; it is cited in later ritual digests.

**Genre:** stotra (devotional hymn)

**Estimated date:** 10th-early 11th c. CE

A short devotional hymn of four verses ('Four Stanzas') in praise of Śrī (Lakṣmī), extolling the goddess's supreme role as the consort of Nārāyaṇa and as the mediatrix who grants grace and liberation to individual souls (jīvas). It is foundational for Śrī Vaiṣṇava theology of Lakṣmī's salvific function.

**History:** Yāmunācārya (traditionally c. 918-1038 CE), grandson of Nāthamuni and predecessor of Rāmānuja, was a key systematizer of Viśiṣṭādvaita. The Catuḥślokī is one of his six works and, with his Stotraratna, established the devotional tone of the tradition that Rāmānuja later elaborated philosophically.

**Related works:** Stotraratna, Siddhitraya, Gītārthasaṅgraha, Āgamaprāmāṇya

The 'Jewel of Hymns', a celebrated devotional poem in praise of Nārāyaṇa (Viṣṇu). It expresses self-surrender (prapatti) and the soul's complete dependence on God's grace, blending intense bhakti with the doctrinal framework of Viśiṣṭādvaita, and opens with homage to the lineage of teachers (Nāthamuni, etc.).

A running commentary (vṛtti) on Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, the oldest surviving complete commentary covering all of Pāṇini's nearly 4000 sūtras in their original sequence. Noted for lucid explanations, illustrative examples, and awareness of earlier grammatical works (Mahābhāṣya, Cāndravyākaraṇa), it makes Pāṇini's cryptic rules accessible.

**History:** Traditionally co-authored by Jayāditya and Vāmana (c. 7th century CE), reportedly with Jayāditya responsible for the first five adhyāyas and Vāmana the rest. It became the standard reference for Pāṇinian study and was itself the basis of the major sub-commentaries Nyāsa (Jinendrabuddhi) and Padamañjarī (Haradatta).

The foundational grammar of Sanskrit, comprising nearly 4000 terse, algebraically organized sūtras in eight chapters (aṣṭa-adhyāyī) that generate correct Sanskrit forms through an ordered system of rules, metarules, and technical conventions. It is the most comprehensive and rigorous descriptive grammar of antiquity and effectively standardized Classical Sanskrit.

**History:** Composed by Pāṇini, probably in the northwest (Śalātura, Gandhāra) around the mid-1st millennium BCE, drawing on earlier grammarians it names. Its rule system is often compared to a formal generative grammar. It was elaborated by Kātyāyana's Vārttikas and Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, and remains the bedrock of the entire Sanskrit grammatical tradition.

**Related works:** Mahābhāṣya, Kāśikāvṛtti, Vārttika (Kātyāyana), Siddhāntakaumudī, Dhātupāṭha, Gaṇapāṭha

The Tattvopaplavasiṃha ('The Lion that Devours All Categories/Principles') is an extraordinary skeptical treatise that systematically demolishes the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas)—perception, inference, and testimony—as accepted by every Indian philosophical school. **History:** The sole palm-leaf manuscript was discovered in 1926 and first published in 1940 by Sukhlalji Sanghavi and R. C. Parikh. Jayarāśi is a uniquely radical figure: though linked to the materialist Cārvāka/Lokāyata, his thoroughgoing skepticism distinguishes him from typical materialists and makes the work a singular monument of Indian anti-foundationalist philosophy.

The Kāmasūtra is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāma (pleasure, desire, love), one of the three legitimate aims of human life. The Rasahṛdayatantra ('Heart of Mercury') is generally regarded as the earliest systematic work of the Sanskrit alchemical genre rasaśāstra. It is one of the most influential Tantric alchemical scriptures and was studied by D. G. White and others for its fusion of Tantra and chemistry.

A foundational, highly condensed Sanskrit treatise on mathematics and astronomy in 121 verses across four sections: Gītikāpāda (astronomical constants), Gaṇitapāda (arithmetic, algebra, geometry, the sine table, series, an approximation of π ≈ 3.1416), Kālakriyāpāda (reckoning of time and planetary longitudes), and Golapāda (spherical astronomy, eclipses). It famously proposes the Earth's axial rotation.

It introduced influential algorithms including the kuṭṭaka (pulverizer). This record is the root (mūla) text.

**Related works:** Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya (Bhāskara I), Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya (Nīlakaṇṭha)

A classic Sanskrit treatise on algebra, forming part of Bhāskara II's larger Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. The Ṛgveda recension of the Vedāṅgajyotiṣa, the oldest surviving Indian astronomical text, here in 36 verses. It provides a calendrical and astronomical framework—a five-year yuga, lunar and solar months, tithis, nakṣatras, intercalation and solstice positions—to fix the correct times for Vedic sacrifices and rituals.

**History:** Traditionally ascribed to the sage Lagadha; it is the jyotiṣa Vedāṅga (one of the six limbs of the Veda). Its solstitial data are used to argue for a late-Vedic date, with traditional estimates ranging c. 1400-1200 BCE and conservative linguistic estimates around the mid-1st millennium BCE; the dating is much debated. The text survives in Ṛk (Ārca) and Yajus recensions.

**Related works:** Yajurvedavedāṅgajyotiṣa, Vedāṅgas, Ṛgveda

The Līlāvatī is the arithmetic-and-geometry section of Bhāskara II's larger astronomical compendium Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. In thirteen chapters it treats arithmetic operations, fractions, proportions, arithmetic and geometric progressions, interest, plane and solid mensuration, gnomon/shadow problems, indeterminate equations (kuṭṭaka), and combinatorics, often framed as charming problems addressed to a girl named Līlāvatī. It is one of the most influential pedagogical mathematics texts of premodern India.

**History:** Composed by Bhāskara II (b. 1114 CE) of the Ujjain astronomical school, the work circulated for centuries as a standard arithmetic primer and was translated into Persian under Akbar (by Faizi, 1587) and later into European languages. Numerous Sanskrit commentaries (e.g. by Gaṇeśa Daivajña) attest to its enduring authority.

**Related works:** Siddhāntaśiromaṇi, Bījagaṇita

The Sūryasiddhānta is one of the foundational Sanskrit treatises of Indian mathematical astronomy, presented as instruction revealed by the Sun-god. In fourteen chapters it covers planetary mean and true motions, eclipses, heliacal risings and settings, the phases of the moon, planetary conjunctions, cosmography, time-reckoning, and the construction of astronomical instruments, and it embeds early sine-table trigonometry.

**History:** The text is a 'living document' revised over centuries; the surviving version differs from the older Sūryasiddhānta paraphrased by Varāhamihira in his Pañcasiddhāntikā. It became the most widely cited and commented astronomical authority in India and underlies much of later Hindu calendrical practice; E. Burgess produced an influential English translation in 1860.

**Related works:** Pañcasiddhāntikā, Siddhāntaśiromaṇi

**History:** No complete manuscript survives; Julius Jolly translated some 700 vyavahāra verses (SBE 33) and K. V. The text closely follows and elaborates Manu, placing it after the Manusmṛti.

The Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā, or Parāśarasmṛti, is a dharmaśāstra in twelve chapters (about 600 verses) that presents itself as the lawbook appropriate to the Kali age (kaliyuga). It concentrates on ācāra (right conduct), the duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, ritual observances, purification, penance, and the merit of charity (dāna) as the supreme virtue for the present age; it largely omits detailed vyavāhara.

**History:** Traditionally each yuga has its own authoritative lawgiver, with Parāśara assigned to the Kali age. The smṛti became influential precisely as a 'Kali-yuga' code and acquired a major commentary, the Parāśaramādhavīya by Mādhavācārya (Sāyaṇa's brother, 14th c.); the date of the base text is disputed.

**Related works:** Manusmṛti, Parāśaramādhavīya (commentary by Mādhava)

Words of YDh verse in the commentary are given in bold (but only partially) There are no hyphens used, unless absolutely necessary for an overly long compound. Lack of hyphens should help with word searches. The transcription was prepared from the Nirnaya Sagar Press edition . In checking the transcription and preparing the edition, I used two other editions: Pāṇḍeya's edition in Kashi Sanskrit Series 178 , and S. S, Setlur's edition of 1912 . Pāṇḍeya's appears to be based on the NSP. The best is Setlur's, which also includes two subcommentaries, Subodhinī and Bālambhaṭṭī . One regular change from the NSP is that Vijñāneśvara almost always has an introduction to each verse. Most often this consists of a substantive sentence. But frequently, the introduction consists of two brief introductions: kiṃ ca , api ca , and infrequently tathā ca . NSP and Pāṇḍeya place these in the commentary after the verse. This is an error. You will find that these are found only when there is no substantive introduction. Setlur is the only one who understood this; he places these connective phrases before the verse. So do I. I have tried to eliminate errors and typos, and to make the text user friendly. To that end, I have sometimes eliminated external sandhi and often introduced punctuation. There are certainly still numerous typos and errors. Kindly inform me or Don Davis so that we may correct them. The transcription of this Sanskrit text was funded by the College of Liberal Arts at the University of Texas at Austin. Donald R. Davis, Jr. (drdj@austin.utexas.edu) and Patrick Olivelle (jpo@austin.utexas.edu) University of Texas at Austin Searchable Electronic Edition of the Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara, a commentary on the Yājñavalkya-dharmaśāstra Edited, formatted, and color coded by Patrick Olivelle Transcribed by Donald Davis (1.1–25); Amy Hyne-Sutherland (1.26—2.80); Nikola Rajić (2.80–3.334) About the Author and the Work The Mitākṣarā , or The Epitome of the Law , by the twelfth-century Sanskrit author Vijñāneśvara is, along with the second-century text the Laws of Manu ( Mānava-dharmaśāstra ), one of the two most influential works of classical Hindu law. Its subject is dharma , legal and religious duty, which Olivelle has described as “the most central feature of Indian civilization down the centuries, irrespective of linguistic, sectarian, or regional differences” ( Dharma , Motilal, 2009: vii). As the premier synthesis of dharma , it thus represents a watershed moment not only in the history of Sanskrit legal and religious thought but also in the intellectual history of India generally. Its genius lies in the clarity and precision of its explanations and in its creative synthesis of earlier jurisprudential thought. Widely disseminated, translated or summarized into several vernacular languages, and elaborated in many subcommentaries, the Mitākṣarā exerted an unparalleled influence on legal thought in medieval and early modern India. Its author, Vijñāneśvara was also known as Vijñānayogin. About Vijñāneśvara’s life, we know only what the colophons to the many surviving manuscripts tell us. He was the son of a teacher named Padmanābha-bhaṭṭa, belonged to the vedic lineage ( gotra ) of the sage Bharadvāja, and was a student of Uttama. He seems to have served at the court of king Vikramāditya VI (d. 1127 CE) of the Cālukya dynasty and perhaps lived in its capital city of Kalyāṇa, today’s Basavakalyan in northeastern Karnataka. He wrote his masterpiece on dharma the form of a commentary on the Laws of Yājñavalkya , an earlier treatise on dharma from the fourth or fifth century CE (see Olivelle, A Treatise on Dharma , Harvard, 2019). This commentary, however, ranges far beyond its source text, authoritatively citing scores of other dharma texts and offering sometimes elaborate new discussions of particular topics. P.V. Kane, the great historian of the Dharmaśāstra genre, likens the significance of the Mitākṣarā “to that of the Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali in grammar or to that of the Kāvyaprakāśa of Mammaṭa in poetics” ( History of Dharmaśāstra , vol. 1, 599). sakalam iti | anyad api śāstroktaṃ jātiguṇahomayāgādi tat sakalaṃ dharmasya kārakaṃ, jātiguṇadravyakriyābhāvārthātmakaṃ caturvidhaṃ dharmasya kārakam ity uktaṃ bhavati | tac ca samastaṃ vyastaṃ vā yathāśāstraṃ draṣṭavyam | śraddhā sarvatrānuvartata eva || 1.6 || idānīṃ dharmasya jñāpakahetūn āha | śrutiḥ smṛtiḥ sadācāraḥ svasya ca priyam ātmanaḥ | samyaksaṃkalpajaḥ kāmo dharmamūlam idaṃ smṛtam || YDh_1.7 śrutir vedaḥ | smṛtir dharmaśāstram | tathā ca manuḥ | śrutis tu vedo vijñeyo dharmaśāstraṃ tu vai smṛtiḥ | iti | (MDh 2.10) sadācāraḥ satāṃ śiṣṭānām ācāro 'nuṣṭhānam | svasya cātmanaḥ priyaṃ , vaikalpike viṣaye yathā garbhāṣṭame 'ṣṭame vābde (YDh 1.14) ityādav ātmecchaiva niyāmikā | samyaksaṃkalpāj jātaḥ kāmaḥ śāstrāviruddhaḥ yathā mayā bhojanavyatirekeṇodakaṃ na pātavyam iti | ete dharmasya mūlaṃ pramāṇam | eteṣāṃ virodhe pūrvapūrvasya balīyastvam || 1.7 || deśādikārakahetūnām apavādam āha | ijyācāradamāhiṃsādānasvādhyāyakarmaṇām | ayaṃ tu paramo dharmo yad yogenātmadarśanam || YDh_1.8 ijyā dināṃ karmaṇām ayam eva paramo dharmaḥ yad yogena bāhyacittavṛttinirodhen ātmano darśanaṃ yāthātathyajñānam | yogenātmajñāne deśādiniyamo nāstīty arthaḥ | tad uktaṃ yatraikāgratā tatrāviśeṣāt (BrSū 4.1.11) iti pātañjale || 1.8 || kārakahetuṣu jñāpakahetuṣu vā saṃdehe tu nirṇayahetum āha | catvāro vedadharmajñāḥ parṣat traividyam eva vā | sā brute yaṃ sa dharmaḥ syād eko vādhyātmavittamaḥ || YDh_1.9 catvāro brāhmaṇāḥ vedadharma śāstra jñāḥ parṣat | tisro vidyā adhīyanta iti traividyāḥ | teṣāṃ samūhas traividyam | dharmaśāstrajñatvam atrāpy anuvartate | tad vā parṣat | sā pūrvoktā parṣat yaṃ brute sa dharmaḥ | adhyātma jñāneṣu nipuṇatamo dharmaśāstrajñaś ca eko 'pi vā yaṃ brute so 'pi dharmaḥ || 1.9 || ity upodghātaprakaraṇam | atha brahmacāriprakaraṇam etair navabhiḥ ślokaiḥ sakalaśāstropodghātam uktvā, idānīṃ varṇādīnāṃ dharmān vaktuṃ prathamaṃ tāvad varṇān āha | brahmakṣatriyaviṭśūdrā varṇās tv ādyās trayo dvijāḥ | niṣekādyāḥ śmaśānāntās teṣāṃ vai mantrataḥ kriyāḥ || YDh_1.10 brāhmaṇakṣatriyavaiśyaśūdrāś catvāro varṇā vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇās, teṣām ādyās trayo brāhmaṇakṣatriyavaiśyā dvijāḥ | dvir jāyanta iti dvijāḥ | teṣāṃ dvijānāṃ vai eva na śūdrasya | etena śūdrasyāmantrakāḥ kriyā ity uktaṃ bhavati | śūdro 'py evaṃvidhaḥ kāryo vinā mantreṇa saṃskṛtaḥ | iti yamo kteḥ | niṣekādyāḥ niṣeko garbhādhānam ādyo yāsāṃ tās tathoktāḥ | śmaśānaṃ pitṛvanaṃ tatsaṃbandhi karma anto yāsāṃ tāḥ kriyā mantrair bhavati || 1.10 || idānīṃ tāḥ kriyā anukrāmati | garbhādhānam ṛtau puṃsaḥ savanaṃ spandanāt purā | ṣaṣṭhe 'ṣṭame vā sīmanto māsy ete jātakarma ca || YDh_1.11 ahany ekādaśe nāma caturthe māsi niṣkramaḥ | ṣaṣṭhe 'nnaprāśanaṃ māsi cūḍā kāryā yathākulam || YDh_1.12 garbhādhānam ity anugatārthaṃ karmanāmadheyam | evaṃ vakṣyamaṇāny api | tad garbhādhānam ṛtau ṛtukāle vakṣyamaṇalakṣaṇe | puṃsavanā khyaṃ karma garbhacalanāt pūrvam | ṣaṣṭhe 'ṣṭame vā māsi sīmanto nnayanam | ete ca dve puṃsavanasīmantonnayane kṣetrasaṃskārakarmatvāt sakṛd eva kārye na pratigarbham | yathāha devalaḥ | sakṛc ca saṃskṛtā nārī sarvagarbheṣu saṃskṛtā | yaṃ yaṃ garbhaṃ prasūyeta sa sarvaḥ saṃskṛto bhavet || iti | yad vā ete ā ite āgate garbhakośāj jāte kumāre jātakarma | ekādaśe 'hani nāma | tac ca pitāmahamātāmahādisaṃbaddhaṃ kuladevatāsaṃbaddhaṃ vā | yathāha śaṅkhaḥ (2.14) kuladevatāsaṃbaddhaṃ pitā nāma kuryāt iti | caturthe māsi niṣkramaṇa lakṣaṇaṃ sūryāvekṣaṇaṃ karma | ṣaṣṭhe māsy annaprāśanaṃ karma | cūḍā karaṇaṃ tu yathākulaṃ | kāryam iti pratyekaṃ saṃbadhyate || 1.11-12 || eteṣāṃ nityatve 'py ānuṣaṅgikaṃ phalam āha | evam enaḥ śamaṃ yāti bījagarbhasamudbhavam | YDh_1.13ab evam uktena prakāreṇa garbhādhānādibhiḥ saṃskārakarmabhiḥ kṛtair enaḥ pāpaṃ śamaṃ yāti | kiṃbhūtaṃ | bījagarbhasamudbhavaṃ śukraśoṇitasaṃbaddhaṃ gātravyādhisaṃkrāntinimittaṃ vā na tu patitotpannatvādi || strīṇāṃ viśeṣam āha | tūṣṇīm etāḥ kriyāḥ strīṇāṃ vivāhas tu samantrakaḥ || YDh_1.13cd etā jātakarmādikāḥ kriyāḥ strīṇāṃ tūṣṇīṃ vinaiva mantrair yathākālaṃ kāryāḥ | vivāhaḥ punaḥ samantrakaḥ kāryaḥ || 1.13 || upanayanakālam āha | garbhāṣṭame 'ṣṭame vābde brāhmaṇasyopanāyanam | rājñām ekādaśe saike viśām eke yathākulam || YDh_1.14 garbhā dhānam ādiṃ kṛtvā jananaṃ vāṣṭame varṣe brāhmaṇasyopanāyanaṃ upanayanam eva upanāyanam | svārthe aṇ | vṛttānusārāt chandobhaṅgāt | ārṣaṃ vā dīrghatvaṃ | atrecchayā vikalpaḥ | rājñām ekādaśe | viśāṃ vaiśyānāṃ saike ekādaśe | dvādaśe ity arthaḥ | garbhagrahaṇaṃ sarvatrānuvartate | samāse guṇabhūtasyāpi garbhaśabdasya buddhyā vibhajyobhayatrāpy anuvartanaṃ kāryam | garbhād ekādaśe rājño garbhāddhi dvādaśe viśaḥ | (Śaṅkh. 2.17) iti smṛtyantara darśanāt | yathā atha śabdānuśāsanaṃ, keṣāṃ śabdānām, laukikānāṃ vaidikānām iti | atrāpi kāryam ity anuvartate | kulasthityā kecid upanayanam icchanti || 1.14 || gurudharmān āha | upanīya guruḥ śiṣyaṃ mahāvyāhṛtipūrvakam | vedam adhyāpayed enaṃ śaucācārāṃś ca śikṣayet || YDh_1.15 svagṛhyoktavidhin opanīya guruḥ śiṣyaṃ mahāvyāhṛtipūrvakaṃ vedam adhyāpayet | mahāvyāhṛtayaś ca bhūrādisatyāntāḥ sapta | pañca vā gautamā bhiprāyeṇa (GDh 1.51)| kiṃ ca śaucācārāṃś ca vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇān śikṣayet | upanīya śaucācārāṃś ca śikṣayed ity anena prāg upanayanāt kāmacāro darśito varṇadharmān varjayitvā | strīṇām apy etatsamānaṃ vivāhād arvāk upanayanasthānīyatvād vivāhasya || 1.15 || śāucācārān āha | divāsaṃdhyāsu karṇasthabrahmasūtra udaṅmukhaḥ | kuryān mūtrapurīṣe ca rātrau ced dakṣiṇāmukhaḥ || YDh_1.16 karṇasthaṃ brahmasūtraṃ yasya sa tathoktaḥ | karṇaś ca dakṣiṇaḥ | pavitraṃ dakṣiṇe karṇe kṛtvā viṇmūtram utsṛjet | iti liṅgāt | asāv ahani saṃdhyayoś ca udaṅmukho mūtrapurīṣe kuryāt | ca kārād bhasmādirahite deśe | rātrau tu dakṣiṇāmukhaḥ || 1.16 || kiṃ ca | gṛhītaśiśnaś cotthāya mṛdbhir abhyuddhṛtair jalaiḥ | gandhalepakṣayakaraṃ śaucaṃ kuryād atandritaḥ || YDh_1.17 anantaraṃ śiśnaṃ gṛhītvotthāyoddhṛtābhir adbhir vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇābhir mṛdbhiś ca gandhalepa yoḥ kṣayakaraṃ śaucaṃ kuryāt | atandrito 'nalasaḥ | uddhṛtābhir adbhir iti jalāntaḥśaucaniṣedhaḥ | atra gandhlepakṣayakaram iti sarvāśramiṇāṃ sādhāraṇam idaṃ śaucam | mṛtsaṃkhyāniyamas tv adṛṣṭārthaḥ || 1.17 || antarjānu śucau deśa upaviṣṭa udaṅmukhaḥ | prāg vā brāhmeṇa tīrthena dvijo nityam upaspṛśet || YDh_1.18 śucau aśucidravyāsaṃspṛṣṭe | deśa ity upādānād upānacchayanāsanādiniṣedhaḥ | upaviṣṭo na sthitaḥ śayānaḥ prahvo gacchan vā | udaṅmukhaḥ prāṅmukho veti digantaranivṛttiḥ | śucau deśe ity etasmāt pādaprakṣālanaprāptiḥ | brāhmeṇa tīrthena vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇena | dvijo na śūdrādiḥ | nityaṃ sarvakālam āśramāntaragato 'pi | upaspṛśed ācāmet | katham | antarjānu jānunor madhye hastau kṛtvā dakṣiṇena hasteneti || 1.18 || prājāpatyāditīrthāny āha | kaniṣṭhādeśinyaṅguṣṭhamūlāny agraṃ karasya ca | prajāpatipitṛbrahmadevatīrthāny anukramāt || YDh_1.19 kaniṣṭḥā yās tarjanyā aṅguṣṭha sya ca mūlāni karasyāgraṃ ca prajāpatipitṛbrahmadevatīrthāni yathākramaṃ veditavyāni || 1.19 || ācamanaprakāraḥ | triḥ prāsyāpo dvir unmṛjya khāny adbhiḥ samupaspṛśet | adbhis tu prakṛtisthābhir hīnābhiḥ phenabudbudaiḥ || YDh_1.20 vāratrayam apaḥ pītvā mukham aṅguṣṭhamūlena dvir unmṛjya khāni chidrāṇi ūrdhvakāyagatāni ghrāṇādīny adbhir upaspṛśet | adbhir dravyāntarāsaṃsṛṣṭābhiḥ | punar adbhir ity abgrahaṇam praticchidram udakasparśanārtham, smṛtyantarāt : aṅguṣṭhena pradeśinyā ghrāṇaṃ caiva mukhaṃ spṛśet | aṅguṣṭhānāmikābhyāṃ ca cakṣuḥśrotraṃ punaḥ punaḥ || kaniṣṭhāṅguṣṭhayor nābhiṃ hṛdayaṃ tu talena vai | sarvābhis tu śiraḥ paścād bāhū cāgreṇa saṃspṛśet || iti | punas tā eva viśinaṣṭi prakṛtisthābhiḥ gandharūparasasparśāntaram aprāptābhiḥ phenabudbuda rahitābhiḥ | tu śabdād varṣadhārāgatānāṃ śūdrādyāvarjitānāṃ ca niṣedhaḥ || 1.20 hṛtkaṇṭhatālugābhis tu yathāsaṃkhyaṃ dvijātayaḥ | śūdhyeran strī ca śūdraś ca sakṛt spṛṣṭābhir antataḥ || YDh_1.21 hṛtkaṇṭhatālugābhir adbhir yathā krameṇa dvijātayaḥ śudhyanti | strī ca śūdraś ca antato ' ntargatena tālunā spṛṣṭābhir api | sakṛd iti vaiśyād viśeṣaḥ | ca śabdād anupanīto 'pi || 1.21 || snānam abdaivatair mantrair mārjanaṃ prāṇasaṃyamaḥ | sūryasya cāpy upasthānaṃ gāyatryāḥ pratyahaṃ japaḥ || YDh_1.22 prātaḥ snānaṃ yathāśāstram abdaivatair mantraiḥ āpo hi ṣṭhā ity evamādibhir mārjanam | prāṇasaṃyamaḥ prāṇāyāmo vakṣyamānalakṣaṇaḥ | tataḥ sūryasyopasthānaṃ sauramantreṇa | gāyatryāḥ tat savitur vareṇyam ityādyāyāḥ pratidivasaṃ japaḥ kāryaḥ | kāryaśabdo yathāliṅgaṃ pratyekam abhisaṃbadhyate || 1.22 || prāṇāyāmavicāraḥ | gāyatrīṃ śirasā sārdhaṃ japed vyāhṛtipūrvikām | pratipraṇavasaṃyuktāṃ trir ayaṃ prāṇasaṃyamaḥ || YDh_1.23 gāyatrīṃ pūrvoktām āpo jyotiḥ ityādinā śirasā saṃyuktāṃ ukta vyāhṛtipūrvikāṃ prati vyāhṛti praṇav ena saṃyuktāṃ oṃ bhuḥ oṃ bhuvaḥ oṃ svar iti trīn vārān mukhanāsikāsaṃcārivāyuṃ nirundhan manasā japed ity ayaṃ sarvatra prāṇāyāmaḥ || 1.23 || sāvitrījapaprakāraḥ | prāṇān āyamya saṃprokṣya tṛcenābdaivatena tu | japann āsīta sāvitrīṃ pratyag ā tārakodayāt || YDh_1.24 saṃdhyāṃ prāk prātar evaṃ hi tiṣṭhed ā sūryadarśānāt | YDh_1.25ab prāṇāyāmaṃ pūrvoktaṃ kṛtvā tṛcenābdaivatena pūrvoktena ātmānam adbhiḥ saṃprokṣya sāvitrīṃ japan pratyak saṃdhyām āsīta | arthāt pratyaṅmukha iti labhyate | ā tārakodayāt tārakodayāvadhi | prāk saṃdhyāṃ prātaḥ samaye evaṃ pūrvoktavidhim ācaran prāṅmukhaḥ sūryodayāvadhi tiṣṭhet | ahorātrayoḥ saṃdhau yā kriyā vidhīyate sā saṃdhyā | tatra ahaḥ saṃpūrṇād ity amaṇḍaladarśanayogyaḥ kālaḥ tadviparītā rātriḥ | yasmin kāle khaṇḍamaṇḍalasyopalabdhiḥ sa saṃdhiḥ | agnikāryaṃ tataḥ kuryāt saṃdhyayor ubhayor api || YDh_1.25cd tataḥ saṃdhyopāsanāntaraṃ dvayoḥ saṃdhyayor agnikāryaṃ agnau kāryaṃ samitprakṣepādi yat tat kuryāt svagṛhyoktena vidhinā || 1.25 || tato 'bhivādayet vṛddhān asāu aham iti bruvan | YDh_1.26ab tadanantaraṃ vṛddhān guruprabhṛtīn abhivādayet | katham | asau devadattaśarm āham iti svaṃ nāma kīrtayan || guruṃ caivāpy upāsīta svādhyāyārthaṃ samāhitaḥ || YDh_1.26cd āhūtaś cāpy adhīyīta labdhaṃ cāsmai nivedayet | hitaṃ tasya acaren nityaṃ manovākkāyakarmabhiḥ || YDh_1.27 tathā guruṃ vakṣyamāṇalakṣaṇam upāsīta tatparicaryāparas tadadhīnas tiṣṭhet | svādhyāyārtham adhyayanasiddhaye samāhito 'vikṣiptacitto bhavet | āhūtaś cāpy adhīyīta gurvāhūta eva adhīyīta na svayaṃ guruṃ prerayet | yac ca labdhaṃ tat sarvaṃ gurave nivedayet | tathā tasya guror hitam ācaret | nityaṃ sadā | manovākkāyakarmabhiḥ na pratikūlaṃ kuryāt | apiśabdād gurudarśane gautamo ktaṃ (GDh 2.14) kaṇṭhaprāvṛtādi varjayet || 1.26 || 1.27 || adhyāpyān āha | kṛtajñādrohimedhāviśucikalyānasūyakāḥ | adhyāpyā dharmataḥ sadhuśaktāptajñānavittadāḥ || YDh_1.28 kṛtam upakāraṃ na vismarati iti kṛtajñaḥ | adrohī dayāvān | medhāvī granthagrahaṇadhāraṇaśaktaḥ | śucir bāhyābhyantaraśaucavān | kalya ādhivyādhirahitaḥ | anasūyako doṣānāviṣkāreṇa guṇāviṣkaraṇaśīlaḥ | sādhur vṛttavān | śaktaḥ śuśrūṣāyām | āpto bandhuh | jñānado vidyāpradaḥ | vittado 'paṇapūrvakam arthapradātā | ete guṇāḥ samastā vystāś ca yathāsaṃbhavaṃ draṣṭavyāḥ | ete ca dharmataḥ śāstrānusāreṇa adhyāpyāḥ || 1.28 || daṇḍādidhāraṇam āha | daṇḍājinopavītāni mekhalāṃ caiva dhārayet | YDh_1.29ab tathā smṛtyantara prasiddhaṃ pālāśādidaṇḍaṃ, ajinaṃ kārṣṇādi, upavītaṃ kārpāsādinirmitaṃ, mekhalāṃ ca muñjādinirmitāṃ, brāhmaṇādir brahmacārī dhārayet | 1.29ab | bhaikṣacaryāprakāraḥ | brāhmaṇeṣu cared bhaikṣam anindyeṣv ātmavṛttaye || YDh_1.29cd ādimadhyāvasāneṣu bhavacchabdopalakṣitā | brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviśāṃ bhaikṣacaryā yathākramam || YDh_1.30 pūrvoktadaṇḍādiyukto brahmacārī brāhmaṇeṣv anindyeṣv abhiśastādivyatirikteṣu svakarmanirateṣu bhaikṣaṃ caret | ātmavṛttaye ātmano jīvanāya na parārthaṃ ācāryatadbhāryāputravyatirekeṇa | nivedya gurave tadanujñāto bhuñjīta | tadabhāve tatputrādau iti niyamāt | atra ca brāhmaṇagrahaṇaṃ saṃbhave sati niyamārtham | yat tu sārvavarṇikaṃ bhaikṣacaraṇam iti tat traivarṇikaviṣayam | yac ca cāturvarṇyaṃ caret bhaikṣam iti tad āpadviṣayam | kathaṃ bhaikṣacaryā kāryā | ādimadhyāvasāneṣu bhavacchadbopalakṣitā | bhavati bhikṣāṃ dehi | bhikṣāṃ bhavati dehi | bhikṣāṃ dehi bhavati ity evaṃ varṇakrameṇa bhaikṣacaryā kāryā || 1.29 || 1.30 || bhojanaprakāraḥ | kṛtāgnikāryo bhuñjīta vāgyato gurvanujñayā | apośanakriyāpūrvaṃ satkṛtyānnam akutsayan || YDh_1.31 pūrvoktena vidhinā bhikṣām āhṛtya gurave nivedya tadanujñayā kṛtāgnikāryo vāgyato mauny a nnaṃ satkṛtya saṃpūjya akutsayann anindan apośanakriyāṃ amṛtopastaraṇam asi ityādikāṃ pūrvaṃ kṛtvā bhuñjīta | atra punar agnikāryagrahaṇaṃ saṃdhyākāle kathaṃcid akṛtāgnikāryasya kālāntaravidhānārthaṃ na punas tṛtīyaprāptyartham || 1.31 || brahmacarye sthito naikam annam adyād anāpadi | brāhmaṇaḥ kāmam aśnīyāc chrāddhe vratam apīḍayan || YDh_1.32 brahmacarye sthita ekānnaṃ nādyād anāpadi vyādhyādyabhāve | brāhmaṇaḥ punaḥ śrāddhe 'bhyarthitaḥ san kāmam aśnīyāt | vratam apīḍayan madhumāṃsaparihāreṇa | atra brāhmaṇagrahaṇaṃ kṣatriyādeḥ śrāddhabhojanavyudāsārtham, rājanyavaiśyayoś caiva naitat karma pracakṣate | iti smaraṇāt || 1.32 || madhumāṃsādivarjyāny āha | madhumāṃsāñjanocchiṣṭaśuktastrīprāṇihiṃsanam | bhāskarālokanāślīlaparivādādi varjayet || YDh_1.33 madhu kṣaudraṃ na madyam | tasya nityaṃ madyaṃ brāhmaṇo varjayet iti niṣedhāt | māṃsaṃ chāgāder api | añjanaṃ ghṛtādinā gātrasya kajjalādinā cākṣṇoḥ | ucchiṣṭam aguroḥ | śuktaṃ niṣṭhuravākyaṃ nānnarasaḥ, tasyābhakṣyaprakaraṇe niṣedhāt | striyam upabhoge | prāṇihiṃsanaṃ jīvavadhaḥ | bhāskara syodayāstamayāva lokanam | aślīlam asatyabhāṣaṇam | parivādaḥ sadasadrūpasya paradoṣasya khyāpanam | ād iśabdāt smṛtyantar oktaṃ gandhamālyādi gṛhyate | etāni brahmacārī varjayet || 1.33 || gurvācāryādilakṣaṇam āha | sa gurur yaḥ kriyāḥ kṛtvā vedam asmai prayacchati | upanīya dadad vedam ācāryaḥ sa udāhṛtaḥ || YDh_1.34 yo 'sau garbhādhānādyā upanayanaparyantāḥ kriyā yathāvidhi kṛtvā vedam asmai brahmacāriṇe prayacchati sa guruḥ | yaḥ punar upanayanamātraṃ kṛtvā vedaṃ prayacchati sa ācāryaḥ || 1.34 || upādhyāyartviglakṣaṇam | ekadeśam upādhyāya ṛtvig yajñakṛd ucyate | ete mānyā yathāpūrvam ebhyo mātā garīyasī || YDh_1.35 vedasy aikadeśaṃ mantrabrāhmaṇayor ekam, aṅgāni vā, yo 'dhyāpayati sa upādhyāyaḥ | yaḥ punaḥ pākayajñādikaṃ vṛtaḥ karoti sa ṛtvik | ete ca gurvācāryopādhyāyartvijo yathāpūrvaṃ yathākrameṇa mānyāḥ pūjyāḥ | ebhyaḥ sarvebhyo mātā garīyasī pūjyatamā || 1.35 || vedagrahaṇārthaṃ brahmacaryāvadhim āha | prativedaṃ brahmacaryaṃ dvādaśābdāni pañca vā | grahaṇāntikam iti eke keśāntaś caiva ṣoḍaśe || YDh_1.36 yadā vivāhāsaṃbhave vedān adhītya vedau vā vedaṃ vā (MDh 3.2) iti pravartate tadā prativedaṃ vedaṃ vedaṃ prati brahmacaryaṃ pūrvoktaṃ dvādaśa varṣāṇi kāryam | aśaktau pañca | grahaṇāntikam iti eke varṇayanti | keśāntaḥ punar godānākhyaṃ karma garbhād ārabhya ṣoḍaśe varṣe brāhmaṇasya kāryam | etac ca dvādaśavārṣike vedavrate boddhavyaṃ | itarasmin pakṣe yathāsaṃbhavaṃ draṣṭavyam | rājanyavaiśyayos tūpanayanakālavad dvāviṃśe caturviṃśe vā draṣṭavyam || 1.36 || upanayankālasya paramāvadhim āha | ā ṣoḍaśād ā dvaviṃśāc caturviṃśāc ca vatsarāt | brahmakṣatraviśāṃ kāla aupanāyanikaḥ paraḥ || YDh_1.37 ata ūrdhvaṃ patanty ete sarvadharmabahiṣkṛtāḥ | sāvitrīpatitā vrātyā vrātyastomād ṛte kratoḥ || YDh_1.38 ā ṣoḍaśād varṣāt ṣoḍaśavarṣaṃ yāvad ā dvāviṃśād ā caturviṃśād varṣād brahmakṣatraviśām aupanāyanika upanayanasaṃbandhī paraḥ kālaḥ | nātaḥ param upanayanakālo 'sti kiṃ tu ata ūrdhvaṃ patanty ete sarvadharmabahiṣkṛtāḥ sarvadharmeṣv anadhikāriṇo bhavanti | sāvitrīpatitāḥ patitasāvitrīkā bhavanti | sāvitrīdānayogyā na bhavanti: vrātyāḥ saṃskārahīnāś ca vrātyastomāt krator vinā | kṛte tu tasminn upanayanādhikāriṇo bhavanti || 1.37 || 1.38 || ādyās trayo dvijāḥ ity uktaṃ | tatra hetum āha | mātur yad agre jāyante dvitīyaṃ mauñjibandhanāt | brāhmaṇakṣatriyaviśas tasmād ete dvijāḥ smṛtāḥ || YDh_1.39 mātuḥ sakāśāt prathamaṃ jāyante mauñjibandhanāt ca dvitīyaṃ janma yasmāt tasmāt ete brāhmaṇakṣatriyavaiśyā dvijā ucyante || 1.139 || vedagrahaṇādhyayanaphalam āha | yajñānāṃ tapasāṃ caiva śubhānāṃ caiva karmaṇām | veda eva dvijātīnāṃ niḥśreyasakaraḥ paraḥ || YDh_1.40 yajñānāṃ śrautasmārtānāṃ tapasāṃ kāyasaṃtāparūpāṇāṃ cāndrāyaṇādīnāṃ śubhānāṃ ca karmaṇām upanayanādisaṃskārāṇām avabodhakatvena veda eva dvijātīnāṃ paro niḥśreyasakaro nānyaḥ | veda eve ti tanmūlakatvena smṛter api upalakṣaṇārtham || 1.40 || grahaṇādhyayanaphalam uktvā idānīṃ kāmyabrahmayajñādhyayanaphalam āha | madhunā payasā caiva sa devaṃs tarpayed dvijaḥ | pitṝn madhughṛtābhyāṃ ca ṛco 'dhīte hi yo 'nvaham || YDh_1.41 yajūṃṣi śaktito 'dhīte yo 'nvahaṃ sa ghṛtāmṛtaiḥ | prīṇāti devān ājyena madhunā ca pitṝṃs tathā || YDh_1.42 sa tu somaghṛtair devāṃs tarpayed yo 'nvahaṃ paṭhet | sāmāni tṛptiṃ kuryāc ca pitṝṇāṃ madhusarpiṣā || YDh_1.43 yo 'nvaham ṛco 'dhīte sa madhunā payasā ca devān pitṝṃś ca madhughṛtābhyaṃ tarpayati | yaḥ punaḥ śaktito 'nvahaṃ yajūṃṣy adhīte sa ghṛtāmṛtair devān pitṝṃś ca madhughṛtābhyāṃ tarpayati | yas tu sāmāny anvaham adhīte sa somaghṛtair devān pitṝṃś ca madhusarpirbhyāṃ prīṇāti | ṛgādigrahaṇaṃ sāmānyena ṛgādimātraprāptyartham || 1.41 || 1.42 || 1.43 || medasā tarpayed devān atharvāṅgirasaḥ paṭhan | pitṝṃś ca madhusarpirbhyām anvahaṃ śaktito dvijaḥ || YDh_1.44 vākovākyaṃ purāṇaṃ ca nārāśaṃsīś ca gāthikāḥ | itihāsāṃs tathā vidyāḥ śaktyādhīte hi yo 'nvaham || YDh_1.45 māṃsakṣīraudanamadhutarpaṇaṃ sa divaukasām | karoti tṛptiṃ kuryāc ca pitṝṇāṃ madhusarpiṣā || YDh_1.46 te tṛptās tarpayanty enaṃ sarvakāmaphalaiḥ śubhaiḥ | YDh_1.47ab yaḥ punaḥ śaktito 'nvaham athavāṅgiraso 'dhīte sa devān medasā pitṝṃś ca madhusarpirbhyāṃ tarpayati | yas tu vākovākyaṃ praśnottararūpaṃ vedavākyaṃ, purāṇaṃ brahmādi, cakārān mānavā didharmaśāstraṃ, nārāśaṃsīś ca rudradaivatyān mantrān, gāthā yajñagāthendragāthādyāḥ, itihāsān mahābhāratā dīn, vidyāś ca vāruṇādyāḥ, śaktito 'anvaham adhīte sa māṃsakṣīraudanamadhusarpirbhir devān pitṝṃś ca madhusarpirbhyāṃ tarpayati || 1.44 || 1.45 || 1.46 || te punas tṛptāḥ santo devāḥ pitaraś ca enaṃ svādhyāyakāriṇaṃ sarvakāmaphalaiḥ śubhair ananyopaghātalakṣaṇair tarpayanti || 1.47ab || praśaṃsārtham āha | yaṃ yam ṛtum adhīte ca tasya tasya āpnuyāt phalam || YDh_1.47cd trir vittapūrṇapṛthivīdānasya phalam aśnute | tapasaś ca parasyeha nityasvādhyāyavān dvijaḥ || YDh_1.48 yasya yasya kratoḥ pratipādakaṃ vedaikadeśam anvaham adhīte tasya tasya kratoḥ phalam avāpnoti | tathā vittapūrṇāyāḥ pṛthivyāḥ triḥ trivāraṃ dānasya yat phalaṃ parasya tapasaś cāndrāyaṇāder yat phalaṃ tad api nityasvādhyāyavān āpnoti | nityagrahaṇaṃ kāmyasyāpi sato nityatvajñāpanārtham || 1.47 || 1.48 || evaṃ sāmānyena brahmacāridharmān abhidhāya, adhunā naiṣṭhikasya viśeṣam āha | naiṣṭhiko brahmacārī tu vased ācāryasaṃnidhau | tadabhāve 'sya tanaye patnyāṃ vaiśvānare 'pi vā || YDh_1.49 anena vidhinā dehaṃ sādhayan vijitendriyaḥ | brahmalokam avāpnoti na ceha jāyate punaḥ || YDh_1.50 uktena prakāreṇātmānaṃ niṣṭhā utkrāntikālaṃ nayatīti naiṣṭikaḥ , sa yāvajjīvam ācāryasamīpe vaset | na vedagrahaṇottarakālaṃ svatantro bhavet | tadabhāve tatputrasamīpe tadabhāve tadbhāryāsamīpe tadabhāve vaiśvānare 'pi | anena uktavidhinā dehaṃ sādhayan kṣapayan vijitendriya indriyajaye viśeṣaprayatnavān brahmacārī brahmalokam amṛtatvam āpnoti | na kadācid iha punar jāyate || 1.49 || 1.50 || iti brahmacāriprakaraṇam atha vivāhaprakaraṇam yaḥ punar vaivāhyas tasya vivāhārthaṃ snānam āha | gurave tu varaṃ dattvā snāyīta tadanujñayā | vedaṃ vratāni vā pāraṃ nītvā hy ubhayam eva vā || YDh_1.51 pūrvoktena nyāyena vedaṃ mantrabrāhmaṇātmakaṃ vratāni brahmacāridharmān anukrāntān ubhayaṃ vā pāraṃ nītvā samāpya gurave pūrvoktāya varam abhilaṣitaṃ yathāśakti dattvā snāyāt | aśaktau tadanujñayā adattavaro 'pi | eṣāṃ ca pakṣāṇāṃ śaktikālādyapekṣayā vyavasthā || 1.51 || snānānantaraṃ kiṃ kuryād ity ata āha | aviplutabrahmacaryo lakṣaṇyāṃ striyam udvahet | ananyapūrvikāṃ kāntām asapiṇḍāṃ yavīyasīm || YDh_1.52 aviplutabrahmacaryo 'skhalitabrahmacaryaḥ | lakṣaṇyāṃ bāhyābhyantaralakṣaṇair yuktāṃ | bāhyāni tanulomakeśadaśanām ityādīni (MDh 3.10) manuno ktāni | ābhyantarāṇi aṣṭau piṇḍān kṛtvā (ĀśGṛ 1.5.5) ityādy āśvalāyano ktavidhinā jñātavyāni | striyaṃ napuṃsakatvanivṛttaye strītvena parīkṣitām | ananyapūrvikāṃ dānenopabhogena vā puruṣāntarāparigṛhītām | kāntāṃ kamanīyāṃ vodur manonayanānandakāriṇīm, yasyāṃ manaścakṣuṣor nirbandhas tasyām ṛddhiḥ ity āpastamba smaraṇāt (ĀpGṛ 1.3.21; BGṛ 2.3.9) | etac ca nyūnādhikāṅgādibāhyadoṣābhāve | asapiṇḍāṃ samāna ekaḥ piṇḍo deho yasyāḥ sā sapiṇḍā na sapiṇḍā asapiṇḍā tām | sapiṇḍatā ca ekaśarīrāvayavānvayena bhavati | tathāhi putrasya pitṛśarīrāvayavānvayena pitrā saha | evaṃ pitāmahādibhir api pitṛdvāreṇa taccharīrāvayavānvayāt | evaṃ mātṛśarīrāvayavānvayena mātrā | tathā mātāmahādibhir api mātṛdvāreṇa | tathā mātṛṣvasṛmātulādibhir api ekaśarīrāvayavānvayāt | tathā pitṛvyapitṛṣvasrādibhir api | tathā patyā saha patnyā ekaśarīrārambhakatayā | evaṃ bhrātṛbhāryāṇām api parasparam ekaśarīrārabdhaiḥ sahaikaśarīrārambhakatvena | evaṃ yatra yatra sapiṇḍaśabdaḥ tatra tatra sākṣāt paramparayā vā ekaśarīrāvayavānvayo veditavyaḥ | yady evaṃ mātāmahādīnām api daśāhaṃ śāvam āśaucaṃ sapiṇḍeṣu vidhīyate | (MDh 5.59) ity aviśeṣeṇa prāpnoti | syāt etad yadi tatra prattānām itare kuryuḥ (VaDh 4.19) ityādiviśeṣavacanaṃ na syāt | ataś ca sapiṇḍeṣu yatra viśeṣavacanaṃ nāsti tatra daśāhaṃ śāvam āśaucam ity etad vacanam avatiṣṭate | avaśyaṃ caikaśarīrāvayavānvayena sāpiṇḍyaṃ varṇanīyam | ātmā hi yajña ātmanaḥ ityādi śruteḥ , tathā prajām anu prajāyase (TaitB 1.5.5.6) iti ca, sa evāyaṃ virūḍhaḥ pratyakṣeṇopalabhyate (ĀpDh 2.24.2) ity āpastamba vacanāc ca | tathā garbhopaniṣadi etat ṣāṭkauśikaṃ śarīraṃ trīṇi pitṛtas trīṇi mātṛto 'sthisnāyumajjānaḥ pitṛtas tvaṅmāṃsarudhirāṇi mātṛtaḥ iti tatra tatrāvayavānvayapratipādanāt | nirvāpyapiṇḍānvayena tu sāpiṇḍye (aṅgīkriyamāṇe) mātṛsaṃtāne bhrātṛpitṛvyādiṣu ca sāpiṇḍyaṃ na syāt | samudāyaśaktyaṅgīkāreṇa rūḍhiparigrahe 'vayavaśaktis tatra tatrāvagamyamānā parityaktā syāt | (satsv Setlur: asatv; the additional text given in Setlur and Pāṇḍeya (Chaukhamba). avayavārtheṣu yo 'nyatrārthe prayujyate tatrānanyagatitvena samudāyaḥ prasiddhati |) paramparayaikaśarīrāvayavānvayena tu sāpiṇḍye yathā nātiprasaṅgas tathā vakṣyāmaḥ | yavīyasīṃ vayasā pramāṇataś ca nyūnāṃ udvahet pariṇayet svagṛhyoktavidhinā || 1.52 || viśeṣāntarāṇy āha | arogiṇīṃ bhātṛmatīm asamānārṣagotrajām | YDh_1.53ab arogiṇīm acikitsanīyavyādhyanupasṛṣṭām | bhātṛmatīṃ putrikākaraṇaśaṅkānivṛttaye | anenāparibhāṣitāpi putrikā bhavatīti gamyate | asamānārṣagotrajām ṛṣer idam
