dharmakāmas tu mahatīṃ śriyam āpnuyāt | yathā gurukratuphalaṃ prāpnoti susamāhitaḥ || YDh_3.327 yas tv abhyudayakāmaḥ prājāpatyādikṛcchrān anutiṣṭhati sa mahatīṃ rājyādilakṣaṇāṃ śriyaṃ vibhūtim anubhavati | yathā gurukratūnāṃ rājasūyādīnāṃ kartā tatphalaṃ svārājyādilakṣaṇaṃ mahat phalaṃ labhate, tathāyam api susumāhitaḥ sakalāṅgakalāpam avikalam anutiṣṭhann iti phalamahimaprakāśanārthaṃ kratudṛṣṭāntakīrtanam | susumāhita ity anenāvikalaśāstrānuṣṭhānaṃ vadan kāmyakarmatayāṅgavaikalye phalāsiddhiṃ dyotayati | ato nātra prāyaścitteṣv iva yāvatsaṃbhavāṅgānuṣṭhānam aṅgīkaraṇīyam iti dūrotsāritaṃ pratyāmnāyopādānam | kṛcchrādyanuṣṭhānāvṛttau tu adhikāriṇaḥ phalāvṛttiḥ karmaṇy ārambhabhāvyatvād iti nyāyalabhyā sthitaiveti nedam avivakṣitam || 3.327 || prāguditākhilārthopasaṃhāravyājena dharmaśāstradhāraṇādividhīn sārthavādān prārthanāvaradānarūpeṇa pratipādayitum āha | śrutvaitān ṛṣayo dharmān yājñavalkyena bhāṣitān | idam ūcur mahātmānaṃ yogīndram amitaujasam || YDh_3.328 atra hi varṇāśramādivyāvṛttā dharmāḥ ṣaṭprakārāḥ pratipāditāḥ tān akhilān yogīśvara bhāṣitān ṛṣayaḥ śrutvā praharṣotphullalocanās taṃ mahimaguṇaśālinam acintanīyaśaktivibhavam idam abhidhāsyamānam ūcivāṃsaḥ || 3.328 || ya idaṃ dhārayiṣyanti dharmaśāstram atandritāḥ | iha loke yaśaḥ prāpya te yāsyanti triviṣṭapam || YDh_3.329 vidyārthī prāpnuyād vidyāṃ dhanakāmo dhanaṃ tathā | āyuṣkāmas tathaivāyuḥ śrīkāmo mahatīṃ śriyam || YDh_3.330 ślokatrayam api hy asmād yaḥ śrāddhe śrāvayiṣyati | pitṝṇāṃ tasya tṛptiḥ syād akṣayyā nātra saṃśayaḥ || YDh_3.331 brāhmaṇaḥ pātratāṃ yāti kṣatriyo vijayī bhavet | vaiśyaś ca dhānyadhanavān asya śāstrasya dhāraṇāt || YDh_3.332 ittham ṛjvarthaiḥ ślokaiḥ sāmaśravaḥprabhṛtayo 'nekadhā prārthayante sma || 3.329 – 3.332 || aparām api prārthanām āha | ya idaṃ śrāvayed vidvān dvijān parvasu parvasu | aśvamedhaphalaṃ tasya tad bhavān anumanyatām || YDh_3.333 yas tv idaṃ dharmaśāstraṃ pratiparva dvijān śrāvayet tasyāśvamedhaphalaṃ bhaved iti śrāvaṇavidhyarthavādaḥ | tad etad asmatprārthitam arthaṃ sarvatra bhavān anumanyatām || 3.333 || varadānam āha | śrutvaitad yājñavalkyo 'pi prītātmā munibhāṣitam | evam astv iti hovāca namaskṛtya svayaṃbhuve || YDh_3.334 etad ṛṣibhir bhāṣitaṃ śrutvā yogīndro 'pi svanirmitadharmaśāstradhāraṇādiphalaprārthanonmīlitamukhapaṅkajaḥ svayaṃbhuve brahmaṇe namaskṛtya praṇamya bhavatprārthitaṃ sakalam itthaṃ bhavatu ity evaṃ kila bhagavān babhāṣe || 3.334 || iti śrībhāradvājapadmanābhabh aṭṭopādhyāyātmajasya śrīmatparamahaṃsaparivrājaka vijñāneśvarabhaṭṭārakasy a kṛtau ṛjumitākṣarāyāṃ yājñavalkyadharmaśāstravivṛttau prāyaścittādhyāyas tṛtīyaḥ samāptaḥ || athātrādhyāyānukramaṇikā likhyate | tatrādyaṃ sūtakaprakraraṇam 1 | āpaddharmaprakaraṇam 2 | vānaprasthaprakaraṇam 3 | adhyātmaprakaraṇam 4 | tataḥ prāyaścittaprakaraṇam 5 | tatrādau karmavipākaḥ 6 | mahāpātakādinimittaparigaṇanam 7 | mahāpātakaprāyaścittāny ātideśikasahitāni 8 | upapātakaprāyaścittāni 9 | prakīrṇakaprāyaścittaprakaraṇam 10 | patitatyāgavidhiḥ 11 | vratagrahaṇavidhiḥ 12 | rahasyaprāyaścittādhikāraḥ 13 | kṛcchrādilakṣaṇam 14 | iti prakaraṇāni || uttamopapadasyeyaṃ śiṣyasya kṛtir ātmanaḥ | dharmaśāstrasya vivṛti rvijñāneśvarayoginaḥ || 1 || iti yājñavalkyamuniśāstragatā vivṛtir na kasya vihitā viduṣaḥ | pramitākṣarāpi vipulārthavatī pariṣiñcati śravaṇayor amṛtam || 2 || gambhīrābhiḥ prasannābhir vāgbhir nyastā mitākṣarā | analpārthābhir alpābhir vivṛtir vihitā mayā || 3 || nāsīd asti bhaviṣyati kṣititale kalyāṇakalpaṃ puraṃ no dṛṣṭaḥ śruta eva vā kṣitipatiḥ śrīvikramārkopamaḥ | vijñāneśvarapaṇḍito na bhajate kiñcānyadanyopamaś cālpaṃ sthiram astu kalpalatikākalpaṃ tad etat trayam || 4 || sraṣṭā vācāṃ madhuravapuṣāṃ vidvadāścaryasīmnāṃ dātārthānām atiśayajuṣām arthisārthārthanāyāḥ | dhyātā murter muravijayino jīvatādārkacandraṃ jetārīṇāṃ tanusahabhuvāṃ tattvavijñānanāthaḥ || 5 || ā setoḥ kīrtirāśe raghukulatilakasyā ca śailādhirājā- dā ca pratyakpayodheścaṭulatimikulottuṅgariṅgattaraṅgāt | ā ca prācaḥ samudrān natanṛpatiśiroratnabhābhāsurāṅghriḥ pāyādācandratāraṃ jagad idam akhilaṃ vikramādityadevaḥ || 6 || antarmukhāni yadi khāni tapas tataḥ kiṃ nāntarmukhāni yadi khāni tapas tataḥ kim | antarbahir yadi hariś ca tapas tataḥ kiṃ nāntarbahir yadi hariś ca tapas tataḥ kim || 7 || samāpteyaṃ samitākṣarā yājñavalkyasmṛtiḥ

The Mitākṣarā is Vijñāneśvara's authoritative commentary on the Yājñavalkyasmṛti. Best known for its doctrine of 'inheritance by birth' (a son acquires an interest in ancestral property at birth) and its treatment of the joint/coparcenary family, it systematizes Hindu personal law on partition, succession, adoption, women's property, and judicial procedure.

**History:** Written by Vijñāneśvara at the Western Cālukya court of Vikramāditya VI at Kalyāṇa, the Mitākṣarā gave rise to the dominant 'Mitākṣarā school' of Hindu law observed across most of India outside Bengal/Assam, and remained central to Anglo-Hindu jurisprudence into the modern era. Its exact date is debated (Kane, Derrett).

**Related works:** Yājñavalkyasmṛti, Dāyabhāga (rival school), Vīramitrodaya

The Yājñavalkyasmṛti is a major verse dharmaśāstra organized into three sections—ācāra (right conduct), vyavāhara (judicial process), and prāyaścitta (penance/expiation). More concise and systematically arranged than the Manusmṛti, it is especially esteemed for its lucid treatment of legal procedure and had a greater influence on medieval Indian judicial practice than Manu.

**History:** Attributed to the Upaniṣadic sage Yājñavalkya, the extant text is a later composition of the dharmaśāstra tradition. It became the base text for the most important medieval commentaries—above all Vijñāneśvara's Mitākṣarā and the Vīramitrodaya—anchoring Hindu personal law.

**Related works:** Manusmṛti, Mitākṣarā, Vīramitrodaya

The Yamasmṛti is one of the minor dharmaśāstra texts, ascribed to Yama (named as a lawgiver already in the Yājñavalkyasmṛti's list). It is devoted largely to penance and expiatory atonement (prāyaścitta) for sins and ritual transgressions, purification, and the rules of śrāddha—the propitiatory rites for the ancestors—along with their theoretical justification.

**History:** Surviving as a short text quoted extensively in medieval digests, the Yamasmṛti exists in differing recensions; its attribution to Yama is traditional, and its precise date cannot be securely fixed.

**Related works:** Manusmṛti, Yājñavalkyasmṛti, Laghuyamasmṛti

The Mokṣopāya ('Means to Liberation') is a large Kashmiri verse work that teaches a radically idealist, world-as-mind philosophy through a frame dialogue in which the sage Vasiṣṭha instructs the young prince Rāma, illustrated by numerous embedded parables and stories. Its critical recovery is associated with the Mokṣopāya Project (J. Hanneder, W. Slaje).

**Related works:** Yogavāsiṣṭha, Laghu-Yogavāsiṣṭha, Rāmāyaṇa

The Mīmāṃsāsūtra (Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-sūtra or Jaiminisūtra) is the root text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā school, an aphoristic treatise on the interpretation of Vedic injunctions and the principles of ritual exegesis. It was commented upon by Śabara (Śābarabhāṣya), whose commentary was in turn expanded by Kumārila and Prabhākara, founding the two main Mīmāṃsā subschools; its hermeneutics deeply influenced Vedānta, Dharmaśāstra, and Indian legal interpretation.

A metrical (śloka) sub-commentary on the opening section (Tarkapāda, MS 1.1) of Śabara's Bhāṣya on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. It became the foundational text of the Bhāṭṭa branch of Mīmāṃsā and attracted major commentaries including Sucaritamiśra's Kāśikā, Pārthasārathi Miśra's Nyāyaratnākara, and Umbeka Bhaṭṭa's Tātparyaṭīkā.

The foundational sutra-text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā darśana, attributed to Jaimini, comprising roughly 2,700-3,000 aphorisms in twelve adhyāyas. It develops a systematic hermeneutics (vākyaśāstra) for interpreting the Veda with respect to dharma understood as ritual obligation, establishing the authority and self-sufficiency of Vedic injunction, the eternal word-meaning relation, and rules for resolving apparent textual conflicts. This record covers adhyāyas 1-7, transmitted together with Śabara's Bhāṣya.

**History:** The earliest of the six orthodox schools' root texts, it is the basis of all later Mīmāṃsā and deeply shaped Indian exegesis, jurisprudence (dharmaśāstra), and Vedānta. Its sole complete extant ancient commentary is the Śābarabhāṣya, itself sub-commented by Kumārila (Bhāṭṭa) and Prabhākara, founding the two main schools of the tradition.

**Related works:** Śābarabhāṣya, Mīmāṃsāślokavārttika, Tantravārttika, Bṛhatī, Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara, Brahmasūtra (Uttara-Mīmāṃsā)

The Tattvacintāmaṇi ('Wish-Fulfilling Jewel of Truth') is the foundational work of Navya-Nyāya ('New Logic'). Organized into four books on the four pramāṇas — perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony — it develops a rigorous technical language for analyzing cognition, relations, and conditions, transforming Indian logic and epistemology.

**History:** Gaṅgeśa of Mithilā inaugurated the Navya-Nyāya movement; the Tattvacintāmaṇi spawned a vast commentarial literature (Raghunātha, Mathurānātha, Jagadīśa, Gadādhara) and dominated Sanskrit scholastic method for centuries.

The Nyāyakusumāñjali ('Offering of a Handful of Flowers of Reasoning') is Udayana's systematic rational defense of theism (īśvaravāda), built in five chapters (stavakas) of kārikās with the author's own prose commentary. Stavaka 1 opens the work by refuting the Mīmāṃsaka and Cārvāka positions that deny the need for a God, defending the reality of adṛṣṭa (unseen moral causation) and the dependence of the moral order on a supreme cause, thereby establishing the necessity of a regulating intelligent agent.

**History:** Udayana, a Maithila logician at the transition from the older Nyāya to Navya-Nyāya, composed the Nyāyakusumāñjali as the most elaborate Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika treatise on the existence of God; it codifies the classic arguments and attracted numerous later commentaries (e.g. by Varadarāja, Vardhamāna, and Haridāsa). It remains the foundational theistic text of the school.

**Related works:** Nyāyakusumāñjali, Ātmatattvaviveka, Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi, Kiraṇāvalī

**History:** Gaṅgeśa of Mithilā founded the Navya-Nyāya ('New Logic') school, and his Tattvacintāmaṇi became the basic text for all later developments; the Vidhivāda within its Śabda book is a much-studied unit on the semantics of injunctions, treated in modern scholarship (e.g. V. The "Heart of the Doctrine of Recognition," a concise manual of twenty sūtras with the author's own prose commentary, summarizing the Pratyabhijñā philosophy for non-specialists. It teaches that the one absolute consciousness (Citi) freely manifests the universe, contracts itself into limited subjects, and is liberated through the recognition (pratyabhijñā) of its own true nature as Shiva.

**History:** Kṣemarāja, the chief disciple of Abhinavagupta, wrote this popularizing digest to make the dense Īśvarapratyabhijñā system of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta accessible. It became, and remains, one of the most widely read introductions to Kashmir Shaivism.

The earliest fully extant systematic text of classical Sāṃkhya, in about 72-73 āryā verses (hence also 'Sāṃkhyasaptati', the seventy). This entry is one of several recensions/editions of the same work in the collection.

It coordinates conflicting Upaniṣadic statements, refutes rival systems (Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhism, Jainism), and treats meditation and the means to liberation. **History:** Attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, it is one of the prasthānatrayī and the single most commented-upon Vedānta text; its extreme brevity made commentary indispensable, spawning the divergent systems of Śaṅkara, Bhāskara, Rāmānuja, Madhva, Nimbārka, Vallabha and others.

This is Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya, his magisterial commentary on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra. It expounds Viśiṣṭādvaita ('qualified non-dualism'), arguing that Brahman (identified with Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa) is the supreme person whose 'body' is composed of the world of sentient souls and insentient matter, which are real and distinct yet wholly dependent on him. It systematically rebuts Śaṅkara's Advaita interpretation of māyā and the doctrine of an attributeless Brahman.

**History:** The Śrībhāṣya is Rāmānuja's most important work and the foundational systematic text of the Śrīvaiṣṇava theological tradition, drawing on the earlier Bodhāyana-vṛtti tradition. It became the authoritative Vedānta reading for the Viśiṣṭādvaita school and generated an extensive sub-commentarial literature (e.g. Sudarśanasūri's Śrutaprakāśikā).

The Āgamaśāstra, better known as the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā, is a verse treatise in four chapters (prakaraṇas) traditionally attached to the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad. It expounds an uncompromising non-dualism: the phenomenal world is unreal like a dream, the self (Ātman) alone is real, and ultimate truth is 'non-origination' (ajātivāda). The fourth chapter (Alātaśānti) deploys Mahāyāna Buddhist terminology and dialectic.

**History:** It is the earliest surviving systematic text of Advaita Vedānta; Gauḍapāda is regarded as the paramaguru (teacher's teacher) of Śaṅkara, who revered him. Scholars debate the unity of the four chapters and the extent and direction of its engagement with Yogācāra and Madhyamaka Buddhism. Śaṅkara (or a follower) wrote a bhāṣya on it.

**Related works:** Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Brahmasūtra, Śaṅkara's Gauḍapādakārikābhāṣya

The Yogasūtra of Patañjali is the foundational text of the Yoga school of Indian philosophy, comprising c. 195 terse aphorisms in four pādas (Samādhi, Sādhana, Vibhūti, Kaivalya). It defines yoga as 'the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind' (cittavṛttinirodha) and expounds the eightfold path (aṣṭāṅga yoga) culminating in liberation (kaivalya) within a Sāṃkhya-derived metaphysics.

**History:** Modern scholarship (e.g. Maas) often treats the sūtras and the Bhāṣya as a single 'Pātañjalayogaśāstra' composed/redacted around 400 CE; the text shows awareness of Buddhist (Vasubandhu-era) ideas. It generated a rich commentarial tradition and is the most authoritative classical statement of yoga.

**Related works:** Yogasūtrabhāṣya, Tattvavaiśāradī (Vācaspati Miśra), Sāṃkhyakārikā

The Mokṣopāya ('Means to Liberation') is the original Kashmirian work that was later reworked into the popular Yogavāsiṣṭha. The Ṛgveda's oral transmission via Saṃhitā- and Padapāṭha is recognized in UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

Madhvācārya's commentary (bhāṣya) on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, interpreting this major Sāmavedic Upaniṣad through the lens of Dvaita (dualist) Vedānta. Madhva reads its teachings—including the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' and the Sat-Vidyā—as affirming an eternal, real distinction between the supreme Lord (Viṣṇu) and the individual soul, against the Advaitic non-dual reading.

**History:** Madhva, the 13th-century founder of the Dvaita school, wrote bhāṣyas on the principal Upaniṣads to support his realist, theistic Vedānta; this one was further elaborated by sub-commentators such as Vyāsatīrtha (the Ṭippaṇī). It is a key polemical and exegetical text of the Mādhva tradition.

**Related works:** Chāndogya-Upaniṣad, Sāmaveda, Brahma-Sūtra-Bhāṣya (Madhva)

A foundational Advaita Vedānta text of 215 verses (kārikās) organized into four chapters (prakaraṇas): Āgama, Vaitathya, Advaita, and Alātaśānti. Expounding the non-duality of Ātman/Brahman, it analyzes the four states of consciousness (waking, dream, deep sleep, and turīya) keyed to the syllable Oṃ, and argues for ajātivāda, the doctrine of non-origination, denying that the world is ever truly created.

**History:** Traditionally ascribed to Gauḍapāda, the paramaguru (teacher's teacher) of Śaṅkara, though his identity and exact date are uncertain. The work, also called the Āgamaśāstra, is celebrated as the earliest systematic exposition of Advaita and is noted for its conspicuous engagement with and absorption of Buddhist (especially Madhyamaka/Yogācāra) terminology and argument; the first chapter circulates intertwined with the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and Śaṅkara wrote a commentary on it.

**Related works:** Māṇḍūkya-Upaniṣad

One of the shortest principal Upaniṣads, comprising 17-18 verses, forming the closing (fortieth) chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda. It teaches that the whole world is pervaded by and to be enveloped in the Lord (īśa), urging renunciation-in-action, the harmonizing of knowledge and ritual works, and a vision of the unity of the Self with all beings.

It is a much-commented text, with bhāṣyas by Śaṅkara and later Vedāntins, and famous opening invocations; two recensions (Kāṇva and Mādhyandina) survive with minor differences.

**Related works:** Śukla Yajurveda, Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā

The principal domestic-ritual manual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda tradition. In aphoristic sūtra style it prescribes the household sacrifices and life-cycle rites (saṃskāras): the daily fire, marriage, conception, birth, name-giving, upanayana (initiation), Vedic study, the new- and full-moon offerings, and funerary observances.

**History:** Attributed to Pāraskara and forming an appendix to Kātyāyana's Śrautasūtra of the Vājasaneyi (Mādhyandina) school. It is one of the most important and widely used gṛhyasūtras, drawing its mantras from the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, and was edited and translated early by Western Indologists (e.g. Stenzler, Oldenberg).

**Related works:** Śukla Yajurveda, Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra

The Advayaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 150 [verses], the Non-Dual') is one of the shorter Prajñāpāramitā sūtras. It presents, in compact form, the Buddha teaching Subhūti the perfection of wisdom understood through non-duality (advaya): emptiness, the non-arising of dharmas, and the realization that wisdom is inseparable from all phenomena. Like other short Prajñāpāramitā texts it distils the central teaching of the larger sutras into a brief, recitable scripture.

It belongs to the broad family of short Perfection of Wisdom sūtras that includes the Heart and Diamond Sutras.

The Śatasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 100,000 Lines') is the largest of the Mahāyāna Perfection of Wisdom sutras. This record (II-1) is the first part of the second major division (parivarta) of the text. The work expounds at vast length the bodhisattva's practice of the six perfections, the emptiness (śūnyatā) and non-substantiality of all dharmas, and the path to omniscient buddhahood, through long dialogues between the Buddha, Subhūti, Śāradvatīputra and Maitreya.

**History:** A later, greatly expanded elaboration of the foundational Aṣṭasāhasrikā (8,000-line) Prajñāpāramitā, developed roughly between the 1st and 4th centuries CE, probably in Gandhāra and northwestern India. It survives in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts and in Tibetan (translated by Yeshe De, c. 8th-9th c.) and Chinese; the threefold division into 100,000/25,000/18,000-line versions is attested from the time of Bodhiruci (6th c.).

**Related works:** Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, Aṣṭadaśasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā

The narrative mounts a pointed anti-Brahmanical, anti-caste polemic—treating the four varṇas as mere conventional designations—and embeds an extensive encyclopedic exposition of pre-Hellenistic Indian nakṣatra (lunar-mansion) astrology and astronomy.

**History:** It is an unusually early and influential avadāna: summarized in Chinese by the Parthian An Shigao in the 2nd century CE and fully translated twice in the 3rd century, it was widely transmitted across Central Asia and Iran. It is valued by historians of science for preserving an early Indian astronomical/astrological system prior to Greek influence.

**Related works:** Divyāvadāna, Mātaṅga-sūtra

The 'Hymn to the Inconceivable [Buddha]' is one of the four hymns making up the Catuḥstava traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna. It praises the Buddha and his awakening while articulating core Madhyamaka doctrines, notably emptiness of own-being (svabhāvaśūnyatā) and dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), presenting ultimate reality as inconceivable and beyond conceptual elaboration.

The Acintyastava is generally accepted as among the more securely Nāgārjunian of the group on doctrinal grounds.

**Related works:** Catuḥstava, Lokātītastava, Niraupamyastava, Paramārthastava, Mūlamadhyamakakārikā

The 'Hymn to the One Who Transcends the World' is the opening hymn of the Catuḥstava ascribed to Nāgārjuna. By its title it appears to compile teachings concerning gestation/conception and the nature of (re)birth in the womb—a theme treated in Buddhist embryological literature that links the suffering of gestation to renunciation—though the work may instead concern garbha in the sense of the buddha-embryo/tathāgatagarbha; the precise content is not securely established here.

**History:** Counted among the minor works of Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and transmitted chiefly in his Tibetan collected writings. Buddhist embryological discourse drew on texts such as the Garbhāvakrāntisūtra, whose original Sanskrit survives only in fragments; this short saṃgraha stands in that broader tradition. Identification of its exact content is tentative.

**Related works:** Collected works of Atiśa, Garbhāvakrāntisūtra (Sūtra on Entry into the Womb)

The 'Fifty Verses on the Guru' is the classic Vajrayana manual on guru devotion, prescribing in detail how a disciple should regard, honor and serve the spiritual teacher. The Caryāmelāpakapradīpa, the 'Lamp for Integrating/Compiling the Practices,' is a systematic prose exposition of the advanced yogas of the Guhyasamāja-tantra as taught in the Ārya (Noble Nāgārjuna) tradition. **History:** Attributed to the 'tantric Āryadeva' of the Guhyasamāja Noble tradition—traditionally identified with the 3rd-century disciple of Nāgārjuna, but actually a much later figure (the work presupposes the developed Guhyasamāja system). It exerted immense influence on Indian and Tibetan Buddhism and was edited and translated by Christian K. Wedemeyer (with the 11th-c. Tibetan translation by Rinchen Zangpo).

**Related works:** Pañcakrama (Nāgārjuna), Guhyasamāja-tantra, Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayana)

**Genre:** sādhana / upadeśa (instructional evocation manual)

**Estimated date:** c. 11th c. CE

An instructional ('upadeśa') sādhana for 'Death-Cheating Tārā,' giving practical oral-style instructions for the White Tārā long-life practice that averts untimely death. It complements the main Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhana with guidance on the visualization, mantra recitation and ritual application for prolonging life.

**History:** Another component of Vāgīśvarakīrti's influential 11th-century Mṛtyuvañcana ('cheating death') White Tārā cycle composed at Vikramaśīla. His death-defeating Tārā instructions became foundational for the Tibetan White Tārā long-life tradition; the text survives in Sanskrit and Tibetan transmission.

**Related works:** Mṛtyuvañcanatārāsādhana, Mṛtyuvañcanasitatārāsādhana, Sādhanamālā, White Tārā long-life cycle

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Mahayana/Vajrayana)

**Genre:** dhāraṇī (apotropaic protective scripture)

**Estimated date:** mid-1st millennium CE (part of the Pañcarakṣā, attested by c. 800 CE)

The 'Great Śītavatī, Queen of Spells' is an apotropaic dhāraṇī scripture and one of the five members of the Pañcarakṣā corpus of protector-goddess incantations. It offers protection against 'cruel' planets, dangerous animals and poisonous insects (and is associated with protection from smallpox), embodied in the goddess Mahāśītavatī, who is affiliated with the Buddha Amitābha.

**History:** Originally circulating under titles such as Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī or Mahā-Daṇḍadhāraṇī-Śītavatī, the text was later incorporated into the Sanskrit Pañcarakṣā collection. The 'five great dhāraṇīs' are attested in Tibetan catalogues from around 800 CE, and over 300 Pañcarakṣā manuscripts survive, mainly from Nepal and eastern India.

**Related works:** Pañcarakṣā, Mahāpratisarā, Mahāsāhasrapramardinī, Mahāmāyūrī, Mahāmantrānusāriṇī

# Guhyavajravilāsinīsādhana

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T02_n1397u`

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T02 (Tantra)

**Source:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC)

**Link:** [https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/342](https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/342)

**Edition:** Benoytosh Bhattacharya (ed.), Sādhanamālā, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 26 & 41, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1925-1928 (the sādhana is one of the 312 in this collection).

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 990 CE – 1107 CE

**Posterior median:** 1049 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayana; yoginī-tantra / Vajrayoginī cult)

**Genre:** sādhana (tantric visualization/evocation manual)

**Estimated date:** c. 10th-12th c. CE

A sādhana for the 'Secret Vajravilāsinī,' a tantric form of the goddess Vajravilāsinī ('Vajra Coquette/Sporting One'), a manifestation associated with the Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī family. It gives the visualization, mantras and evocation rituals for realizing union with this fierce-yet-blissful female deity of the highest (yoginī) tantras.

**History:** Such sādhanas belong to the Vajrayoginī sādhana corpus that developed in eastern India and Nepal between roughly the 10th and 12th centuries, preserved in palm-leaf Sanskrit collections like the Sādhanamālā and the Guhyasamayasādhanamālā, which gather works on the many forms of the goddess by various, often unnamed, authors.

**Related works:** Sādhanamālā, Guhyasamayasādhanamālā, Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī sādhana literature

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; Indo-Nepalese tantric)

**Genre:** tantra / tantric ritual text

**Estimated date:** uncertain; likely later 1st millennium to early 2nd millennium CE

A Buddhist tantric work whose title ('Garland of Secrets/Secret Garland') points to an esoteric ritual or doctrinal compilation in the Vajrayāna mode. It belongs to the body of Sanskrit tantric texts preserved chiefly in Nepalese manuscript collections, dealing with secret (guhya) practice, mantra and meditation.

**History:** The text is obscure and not the subject of a major critical edition; it survives within the Sanskrit Buddhist tantric corpus transmitted by the Newar Buddhist community of the Kathmandu Valley, the principal preserver of Indian Vajrayāna manuscripts after the decline of Buddhism in India. Its precise authorship, date and affiliation remain unestablished.

**Related works:** Buddhist tantric literature, Guhyasamāja Tantra

# Kāṇhapādasya Dohākoṣa

**95% credible interval:** 764 CE – 860 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; mahāsiddha / Sahajayāna tradition)

**Genre:** dohā (mystic song-couplets); tantric realization poetry

**Estimated date:** c. late 8th-early 9th c. CE (author c. 775-850 CE)

The 'Treasury of Dohās' attributed to the mahāsiddha Kāṇha (Kṛṣṇacaryāpāda), a collection of rhymed couplets in Apabhraṃśa expressing the spontaneous (sahaja) experience of awakening and critiquing external ritual and scholasticism. Commentators read the verses as an esoteric manual on advanced yogic practices such as karmamudrā, caṇḍālī (gtum mo) and prabhāsvara (clear light).

**History:** Kāṇha, one of the eighty-four mahāsiddhas and a disciple of Jālandhara, is also among the named poets of the Caryāpada corpus; his name is entangled with that of other 'Kṛṣṇa/Kanha' figures across different lineages. The dohās survive with Sanskrit/Apabhraṃśa commentaries (e.g. by Amṛtavajra) and were preserved in Nepalese manuscripts and in Tibetan translation.

**Related works:** Caryāgītikoṣa, Sarahapādasya dohākoṣa, Dohākoṣaṭīkā (commentaries)

_Web summary confidence: high_

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; Yoginītantra / Anuttarayoga class)

**Genre:** sādhana (tantric evocation/meditation manual)

**Estimated date:** c. 10th-12th c. CE

A ritual 'means of accomplishment' (sādhanopāyikā) for the deity Mahāmāyā, prescribing the self-visualization and worship of the four-faced, four-armed blue heruka Mahāmāyā embracing the consort Buddhaḍākinī, surrounded by yoginīs. It gives the iconographic detail, mantras and meditative sequence needed to realize the deity according to the Mahāmāyā Tantra.

**History:** The work belongs to the practice literature that grew up around the Mahāmāyā Tantra, one of the earliest Yoginī tantras, and is preserved within the Indo-Nepalese Sanskrit sādhana collections (e.g. of the Sādhanamālā type) and the Tibetan Tengyur. Authorship of individual Mahāmāyā sādhanas varies and is often uncertain.

**Related works:** Mahāmāyātantra, Sādhanamālā

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T02_n1402u`

**95% credible interval:** 840 CE – 959 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; Yoginītantra / Anuttarayoga / Yoganiruttara class)

**Genre:** tantra (revealed esoteric scripture)

**Estimated date:** c. late 9th-early 10th c. CE

A short Buddhist Anuttarayoga tantra of the Yoginī class, in three chapters, centered on the deity Mahāmāyā, 'queen of the ḍākinīs and yoginīs,' and especially associated with Dream Yoga. It treats siddhis, the classification of cause/result/means (hetu, phala, upāya) tantras, deity manifestation and maṇḍala, and transgressive techniques for manipulating the subtle body.

**History:** Considered one of the earliest Yoginī tantras: it postdates the Guhyasamāja Tantra (by intertextual evidence) yet predates the more developed Hevajra Tantra. It was translated into Tibetan by the paṇḍita Jinavara with the translator Gö Lhetsé in the 11th century and remains a yidam practice in the Shangpa Kagyü tradition.

**Related works:** Mahāmāyāsādhanopāyikā, Guhyasamāja Tantra, Hevajra Tantra

**95% credible interval:** 734 CE – 911 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; mahāsiddha / Mahāmudrā / Sahajayāna)

**Genre:** dohā (mystic song-couplets); tantric realization poetry

**Estimated date:** c. late 8th-early 9th c. CE

The 'Treasury of Dohās' of Saraha, a celebrated collection of Apabhraṃśa couplets (in Tibet the 'Songs for the People') voicing the spontaneous, innate (sahaja) experience of mind's nature and the Mahāmudrā realization, while satirizing brahmanical ritual, ascetic extremes and dry scholasticism. It is foundational poetry for the Mahāmudrā tradition.

**History:** Saraha is revered as the human source of the Mahāmudrā teachings, preserved above all by the Tibetan Kagyü school. An early manuscript of his Dohākośa was copied in Nepal Saṃvat 221 (1101 CE), among the earliest witnesses, attesting wide circulation of his verses by then.

**Related works:** Kāṇhapādasya dohākoṣa, Caryāgītikoṣa, Mahāmudrā Upadeśa

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; Yoginītantra / Cakrasaṃvara cycle)

**Genre:** sādhana (tantric evocation/meditation manual)

**Estimated date:** c. 10th-12th c. CE

A 'means of accomplishment' for the tantric goddess Vajravārāhī (a form of Vajrayoginī), guiding the practitioner to visualize the red, sow-headed deity at the center of her maṇḍala, recite her mantra and seed-syllable (vaṃ), and identify with her embodiment of wisdom-emptiness and great bliss. The four lotus-petal goddesses Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā and Rūpiṇī attend her.

**History:** Vajravārāhī sādhanas form a major strand of the Cakrasaṃvara/Vajrayoginī practice literature; a well-known example is the Vajravārāhī Sādhana of Umāpatideva (a thirty-seven-goddess maṇḍala), edited and studied by Elizabeth English. Many such sādhanas circulated in the Sanskrit sādhana collections and the Tibetan canon.

**Related works:** Cakrasaṃvara Tantra, Vajrayoginī sādhanas, Sādhanamālā

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; mahāsiddha / Sahajayāna)

**Genre:** caryāgīti (tantric performance-songs); realization poetry anthology

**Estimated date:** c. 8th-12th c. CE (songs composite); manuscript discovered 1907

An anthology of about forty-seven to forty-nine 'songs of conduct/realization' (caryāgīti) in Apabhraṃśa/Old Bengali, composed by various mahāsiddhas, sung as expressions of the enlightened state. Using vivid metaphor and coded 'twilight language,' they treat existence, delusion, the subtle body and the path to liberation, accompanied by a Sanskrit commentary.

**History:** The collection (also linked to the Caryācaryāviniścaya) was recovered in 1907 from the Nepal Royal Library by Haraprasad Shastri and is celebrated as the earliest specimen of Bengali, Assamese, Maithili and Odia literature. The standard scholarly study is Per Kværne's An Anthology of Buddhist Tantric Songs.

**Related works:** Charyapada / Caryācaryāviniścaya, Sarahapādasya dohākoṣa, Kāṇhapādasya dohākoṣa

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; Guhyasamāja / Anuttarayoga tantra)

**Genre:** maṇḍalavidhi (ritual manual for maṇḍala construction and consecration)

**Estimated date:** c. 9th-11th c. CE

A ritual manual setting out the procedures for constructing, consecrating and entering the maṇḍala of the Guhyasamāja deity (Akṣobhyavajra/Samantabhadra and his retinue), including site preparation, deity placement, initiation (abhiṣeka) and offerings. It serves the generation-stage practice of the Guhyasamāja system.

**History:** Maṇḍalavidhi texts form an essential genre of the Guhyasamāja exegetical corpus, transmitted through the Ārya (Nāgārjuna) and Jñānapāda lineages; the Tengyur preserves a large cluster of Guhyasamāja-related maṇḍala-ritual works (Toh 1796-1825). A famous example is Dīpaṃkarabhadra's Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi.

**Related works:** Guhyasamāja Tantra, Piṇḍīkṛtasādhana, Pañcakrama

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Vajrayāna; Yogācāra-Madhyamaka background)

**Genre:** philosophical-tantric treatise (siddhi text)

**Estimated date:** c. 8th c. CE (if by Śāntarakṣita, 725-788 CE); disputed

A tantric treatise establishing 'reality/the true nature' (tattva), engaging the relationship between tantric praxis (mantra, deity yoga, the use of transgressive means) and Buddhist epistemology and Madhyamaka view. It argues for the validity and supremacy of the tantric path while grounding it in established Buddhist philosophy.

**Estimated date:** c. 9th-10th c. CE (traditionally ascribed to the 2nd-c. Nāgārjuna, but the tantric author is a much later figure)

The Pañcakrama ('Five Stages') is the foundational text of the Ārya school's interpretation of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama/utpannakrama) of the Guhyasamāja Tantra. It sets out the advanced yogic stages that lead to buddhahood: speech isolation (vajrajāpa), mind isolation (cittaviśuddhi), the illusory body (māyādeha), clear light (prabhāsvara), and union (yuganaddha). It treats the manipulation of the subtle body, winds (prāṇa) and mind to realize the union of ultimate and conventional truth.

**History:** Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna, who is said to have received the Guhyasamāja from Saraha; modern scholarship dates the tantric Nāgārjuna and this corpus to roughly the 9th-10th century. Together with the Piṇḍīkramasādhana it became the authoritative basis of the Ārya tradition, hugely influential through Candrakīrti, Nāropā and later Tsongkhapa, who wrote 'A Lamp to Illuminate the Five Stages'.

**Related works:** Guhyasamāja Tantra, Piṇḍīkrama / Piṇḍīkramasādhana, Pradīpoddyotana (Candrakīrti)

The Piṇḍīkrama (also Piṇḍīkṛta-sādhana / Piṇḍīkramasādhana) is the Ārya school's principal manual for the generation stage (utpattikrama) of Guhyasamāja practice. It gives instructions for visualizing the Guhyasamāja maṇḍala, generating oneself as the deities, and performing their ritual activities, opening with the statement that the goal of the generation stage is to purify the mind of conceptualizations (vikalpa), the source of delusion.

**History:** Traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna and transmitted as the 'first krama' of the Pañcakrama, though now generally regarded as a separate work composed around the 9th-10th century. With the Pañcakrama it forms the twin foundation of the Ārya exegesis of the Guhyasamāja; studied by R. Wright and others.

**Related works:** Guhyasamāja Tantra, Pañcakrama

It was later incorporated into the Pañcarakṣā collection; the deity Mahāpratisarā is depicted surrounded by the four other protector goddesses.

A celebrated verse work, 'Entering the Way of the Bodhisattva,' guiding the practitioner through the cultivation of the awakening mind (bodhicitta) across ten chapters, covering confession, the gift of bodhicitta, vigilance, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom. A versified 'Introduction to the Middle Way' that presents Madhyamaka philosophy structured around the ten bodhisattva stages (bhūmis) corresponding to the ten perfections (pāramitās). Its sixth chapter, on the perfection of wisdom, contains Candrakīrti's celebrated refutation of intrinsic existence (svabhāva), his critique of Yogācāra mind-only and of Bhāvaviveka's autonomous-inference method, and his sevenfold analysis of the self (the 'chariot' argument).

The Sanskrit of the verses largely survives; the bhāṣya is preserved mainly in Tibetan.

The first chapter of Candrakīrti's 'Clear Words' commentary on Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, commenting on the opening 'examination of conditions' (pratyaya-parīkṣā). It is famous for Candrakīrti's methodological defense of the Prāsaṅgika reductio method against Bhāvaviveka's use of autonomous syllogisms, and his analysis of the four conditions and the denial of arising from self, other, both, or neither.

**History:** Chapter 1 of the Prasannapadā is the most studied and philosophically pivotal portion, as it stages the Prāsaṅgika-Svātantrika debate; it has been edited and translated repeatedly (e.g. by Stcherbatsky, May, and others). The full Prasannapadā is the only Sanskrit commentary on the MMK to survive complete.

**Related works:** Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, Prasannapadā [Madhyamakaśāstravṛtti]

The 'Treatise of the Hand-grasp/Handful' (also rendered Hastavālanāmaprakaraṇa), a very short verse treatise with its own commentary (vṛtti) arguing that ordinary objects, like a snake mistakenly seen in a coiled rope, are merely conceptual imputations lacking real existence when analyzed. The 'Verses on the Essential Meaning' (or 'Collected-Meaning Verses'), a collection of canonical gāthās embedded in the Yogācārabhūmi together with their exegesis, organizing earlier scriptural verses around fundamental Buddhist doctrinal topics. It functions as a structured anthology that interprets received verse-material within the Yogācāra framework.

The 'Analysis of the Jeweled Lineage,' also called the Uttaratantra, the principal Indian śāstra on buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) theory, expounding seven 'vajra topics' — the Three Jewels, the buddha-element/disposition present in all beings, awakening, the qualities of a buddha, and buddha-activity. Composed probably in the 5th century, it is the only tathāgatagarbha treatise surviving in Sanskrit, was translated into Chinese by Ratnamati (early 6th c.), and became central to East Asian and Tibetan buddha-nature thought.

A verse treatise (kārikā) 'Establishing [the Existence of] External Objects' that argues for the reality of external objects of cognition against Yogācāra idealism. Śubhagupta engages critically with Diṅnāga and Vasubandhu, defending the existence of mind-independent atoms/objects while holding a distinctive view that the images (ākāra) of those objects do not themselves appear in cognition. His position oscillates between Sautrāntika and Vaibhāṣika realism.

Śubhagupta was a notable opponent targeted in the Bahirarthaparīkṣā section of Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha and Kamalaśīla's commentary, which helps fix his date to the 8th century. The text is a key source for the Buddhist realist defense of external objects in the perception debate.

**Related works:** Tattvasaṅgraha, Pramāṇavārttika, Viṃśatikā

A monumental encyclopedic foundational text of the Yogācāra school describing the spiritual states, practices, and fruits along the path to Buddhahood. An early Buddhist anthology of aphoristic verses ('utterances', udāna) attributed to the Buddha and his disciples, organized into topical chapters (varga). **Tradition:** Buddhist (Mahāyāna, Madhyamaka)

**Genre:** philosophical treatise / didactic epistle (rajaparikatha, advice to a king)

**Estimated date:** c. 2nd-3rd c. CE (with Nāgārjuna; disputed)

The 'Precious Garland' (also Ratnāvalī rājaparikathā) is a verse work of advice addressed to a king that interweaves Madhyamaka philosophy (emptiness, the two truths, dependent origination) with ethical, political, and religious counsel on righteous governance and the bodhisattva path. It uniquely combines subtle metaphysics with worldly statecraft.

**History:** Attributed to Nāgārjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school, whose dates and even number remain debated (1st-3rd c. CE). It is one of his most accessible works and survives partly in Sanskrit and fully in Tibetan and Chinese; it is counted among his epistolary/advisory writings alongside the Suhṛllekha.

**Related works:** Mūlamadhyamakakārikā, Suhṛllekha

A short Madhyamaka treatise on 'transmigration of existence' (bhavasaṃkrānti) that addresses how rebirth and the passage from one existence to another can occur in the absence of any permanent self or transferable entity, explaining karmic continuity in terms of emptiness and dependent origination.

**History:** Attributed to Nāgārjuna and associated with the corpus of Madhyamaka logical works; the Bhavasaṃkrānti (sūtra and śāstra) was edited by N. A. Sastri (Adyar Library, 1938). Its authorship and date, like several minor works ascribed to Nāgārjuna, are debated.

An alternate/variant version of Candragomin's 'Letter to a Disciple,' an ornate verse epistle expounding Buddhist doctrine, the sufferings of saṃsāra, and the bodhisattva path. **Tradition:** Buddhist (Mahāyāna)

**Estimated date:** c. 5th-7th c. CE (commonly 5th c.; debated)

The 'Letter to a Disciple' is a short, highly ornate kavya in epistolary form that sets out Buddhist teaching on impermanence, the perils of saṃsāra, the rarity of the human birth, and the bodhisattva's compassionate path. It is framed as an exhortation to a disciple who had abandoned his vows for a love affair.

**History:** Composed by the lay scholar and grammarian Candragomin (dated variously 5th-7th c. CE), it is considered the most refined extant Buddhist epistle. The Sanskrit survives (Cambridge and other manuscripts) and was edited by Minaev and later Michael Hahn.

**Related works:** Suhṛllekha (Nāgārjuna), Bodhisattvasaṃvaraviṃśaka (Candragomin)

The 'Spotless Jewel Letter' is an epistle of ethical and religious guidance addressed to the Pāla king Nayapāla of Magadha, offering a collection of moral maxims rooted in bodhisattva ideals and Buddhist moral philosophy for the conduct of a devout ruler.

**History:** Composed by Atiśa Dīpaṅkara Śrījñāna, the influential 11th-century master who later revitalized Buddhism in Tibet, at the request of King Nayapāla. The Sanskrit original is lost; it survives in Tibetan and has been reconstructed into Sanskrit with translation by modern scholars.

A detailed commentary on Dharmakīrti's Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason'), a short treatise on the logical reason/probans (hetu) in Buddhist inference. **History:** Composed by the Buddhist logician Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa (8th c.), it is a key link in the post-Dharmakīrti pramāṇa tradition. It was transmitted with the later sub-commentary Āloka of Durveka Miśra and edited together at Baroda in 1949.

**Estimated date:** c. first half of the 11th c. CE (Ratnakīrti fl. c. 1000-1050)

A concise treatise establishing the Buddhist apoha ('exclusion') theory of meaning, according to which words and concepts do not refer to real universals but pick out their objects negatively, by exclusion of what they are not (e.g. 'cow' = 'not non-cow'). It defends Dignāga's and Dharmakīrti's nominalist semantics against realist (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā) accounts of universals and verbal reference.

**History:** Ratnakīrti was a student of Jñānaśrīmitra at Vikramaśīla and one of the last great figures of the Indian Buddhist logico-epistemological tradition; his short 'siddhi' tracts survive in the Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī collection. The Apohasiddhi distills and systematizes Jñānaśrīmitra's longer Apohaprakaraṇa and is a key source for the mature Buddhist theory of exclusion.

**Related works:** Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, Apohaprakaraṇa (Jñānaśrīmitra), Pramāṇasamuccaya (Dignāga), Pramāṇavārttika (Dharmakīrti)

A proof of the doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga): the thesis that whatever exists is causally efficient and therefore arises and perishes in a single instant, so that all phenomena are radically impermanent. Ratnakīrti develops the argument from existence/causal efficacy (sattvānumāna) against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā defenders of enduring substances and selves.

It is a culmination of centuries of Buddhist–Nyāya debate over momentariness initiated by Dharmakīrti and is widely studied in modern scholarship (Feldman & Phillips translation).

**Related works:** Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi vyatirekātmikā, Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī, Pramāṇavārttika (Dharmakīrti), Kṣaṇabhaṅgādhyāya (Jñānaśrīmitra)

A short polemical treatise ('Refutation of the Whole') denying the reality of the avayavin, the partite whole that Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika realists posit as a distinct substance inhering in and over its parts. Paṇḍita Aśoka argues that the alleged whole is unperceived and incoherent, so that only the atoms/parts (or momentary particulars) are real, supporting the Buddhist reductionist and nominalist ontology.

The Sanskrit text survives and has been edited and translated (e.g. by Tola and Dragonetti); together with his Sāmānyadūṣaṇa it represents a sharp later-Buddhist attack on Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika realism about wholes and universals.

**Related works:** Sāmānyadūṣaṇadikprasāritā, Pramāṇavārttika (Dharmakīrti)

The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is the collected corpus of the short philosophical tracts (nibandhas) of Ratnakīrti, including the Apohasiddhi, the two Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi recensions, the Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa, the Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa, the Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, the Santānāntaradūṣaṇa, and others. They have been intensively studied in modern scholarship (e.g. Parimal Patil, McAllister).

**Related works:** Apohasiddhi (Ratnakīrti), Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi (Ratnakīrti), Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa, works of Jñānaśrīmitra

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Yogācāra and pramāṇavāda / late Indian epistemological school)

**Genre:** philosophical treatise (prakaraṇa, part of the Nibandhāvalī)

**Estimated date:** c. 980-1040 CE (Jñānaśrīmitra, early 11th c.)

The 'Secret of Non-Perception' is a treatise on anupalabdhi — the inference of the absence (abhāva) of a perceptible thing from its non-perception. Jñānaśrīmitra refines Dharmakīrti's theory of how non-cognition can serve as a valid means of knowing absence, against rival accounts of negation.

**History:** One of the monographs forming Jñānaśrīmitra's Nibandhāvalī. It was critically edited and studied (with the Sarvaśabdābhāvacarcā) by Birgit Kellner, who surveyed his anupalabdhi-theory. It is a major late-Buddhist contribution to the epistemology of negation.

**Related works:** Nibandhāvalī (Jñānaśrīmitra), Nyāyabindu (Dharmakīrti), Sarvaśabdābhāvacarcā (Jñānaśrīmitra)

The 'Proof of Momentariness via the Negative Concomitance', one of two complementary proofs (the other being anvayātmikā, positive correlation) that Ratnakīrti gives for the doctrine that all existents are momentary (kṣaṇika). The vyatireka form argues that whatever is not momentary cannot have causal efficacy and hence cannot exist, defending universal momentariness against Nyāya critics.

**History:** Ratnakīrti, a pupil of Jñānaśrīmitra at Vikramaśīla, condensed and sharpened his teacher's arguments. The text was edited in the Six Buddhist Nyāya Tracts (Haraprasad Shastri) and the Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī (A. Thakur); it was translated and studied by A. C. Senape McDermott.

**Related works:** Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Anvayātmikā (Ratnakīrti), Nibandhāvalī (Jñānaśrīmitra), Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī

**Estimated date:** c. 600-660 CE

A short treatise ('Proof of the Existence of Other Mindstreams/Continua') addressing the Buddhist version of the problem of other minds. Dharmakīrti argues that knowledge of other sentient beings' minds is inferred from observed bodily movements and speech that one knows, by analogy with one's own case, to be caused by intention; he further argues that the Yogācāra idealist can justify belief in other minds by the same argument from analogy that the realist uses.

**History:** One of Dharmakīrti's two minor works (alongside the Sambandhaparīkṣā), difficult to place within the sequence of his seven epistemological treatises. The Sanskrit is largely lost; the text survives chiefly in Tibetan translation and was the subject of a commentary by Vinītadeva.

**Related works:** Pramāṇavārttika, Pramāṇaviniścaya, Sambandhaparīkṣā, Nyāyabindu

One of the oldest treatises on the canons of Indian painting and image-making, ascribed to the sage Nagnajit. It sets out the principles of portraiture, iconometry (proportional measurements), and the rules for depicting figures, framed in a dialogue/origin narrative of the art of painting.

The Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā Dṛṣṭāntapaṅkti ('Garland of Examples Adorned by Poetic Fancy') is a Sanskrit collection of around 90 illustrative stories (dṛṣṭānta/avadāna) that teach Buddhist morality, piety toward the Three Jewels, and ethical conduct, often interwoven with concerns for social respectability and prudent worldly action. It is a major example of early ornate Buddhist narrative literature from Gandhāra.

**History:** Composed by Kumāralāta, a Gandhāran monk from Taxila regarded as the first teacher (mūlācārya) of the Sautrāntikas, the work was long misattributed to Aśvaghoṣa under the title Sūtrālaṃkāra. The complete text survives only in Kumārajīva's early-5th-century Chinese translation (Dà zhuāngyán lùn, T201); Sanskrit fragments were recovered at Kizil and edited by Heinrich Lüders (1926).

**Related works:** Sūtrālaṃkāra (mistaken attribution to Aśvaghoṣa), Dà zhuāngyán lùn (Taishō 201, Chinese translation)

**History:** Composed by the emperor Harṣa, who turned from Śaivism toward Mahāyāna Buddhism, it is his only full nāṭaka (his Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā are lighter nāṭikās) and a key example of Buddhist-themed classical drama. It contains an early reference to the practice of satī.

Volume 1 of the Ahirbudhnyasaṃhitā, a major Pāñcarātra scripture cast as a dialogue revealed by Ahirbudhnya (a form of Śiva/Rudra) to Nārada. It expounds Pāñcarātra cosmology and metaphysics (the vyūhas, śakti, the unfolding of the cosmos from Viṣṇu-Nārāyaṇa), as well as mantra-śāstra, the Sudarśana cakra, ritual, yoga and even statecraft/weaponry.

**History:** One of the most important and philosophically rich Pāñcarātra Saṃhitās; F. O. Schrader's 'Introduction to the Pāñcarātra and the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā' (1916) made it a key text for Western study of the tradition. Its date is much disputed and the text is likely composite, accreted over several centuries.

**Related works:** Lakṣmītantra, Jayākhyasaṃhitā, Pāñcarātra Saṃhitā corpus

It was edited and studied by W. A. Borody and others.

The Īśvarasiddhi ('Proof of the Lord') is one of the three short demonstrative treatises (Siddhitrayī) of Utpaladeva, the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') philosopher of nondual Kashmir Shaivism. It argues for the existence of Īśvara (Śiva) as the supreme conscious Subject (the highest 'I'), the ground of all cognition and being. Together with the Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi and Sambandhasiddhi it supplements his major work, the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā.

**History:** Utpaladeva was a pupil of Somānanda and the teacher of the lineage that culminated in Abhinavagupta, who built the Pratyabhijñā system into the philosophical core of Trika Shaivism. The Siddhitrayī survives with Utpaladeva's own auto-commentary (vṛtti); his works were later somewhat overshadowed by Abhinavagupta's more elaborate exegesis.

**Related works:** Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi, Sambandhasiddhi, Śivadṛṣṭi (of Somānanda)

The Kaulajñānanirṇaya ('Ascertainment of Kaula Gnosis') is the foundational scripture of the Yoginī Kaula school attributed to Matsyendranātha. In some 24 sections (paṭalas) it expounds the meaning of kula, Śiva-Śakti nonduality, bindu and nāda, modes of worship, the acquisition of yogic powers (siddhis), and esoteric—often erotic and 'left-handed'—practices for liberation, written in deliberately veiled 'twilight language.'

**History:** Edited from a Nepalese manuscript by P. C. Bagchi (1934), it is a key witness to early Kaula Tantra. Although its author already knew earlier Kaula scriptures (the 'Kulāgama'), Matsyendranātha is celebrated as a founder of Kaulism; Abhinavagupta honored him as a patriarch of yoga. It is central to the Nātha and Yoginī Kaula traditions.

**Related works:** Jñānakārikā, Akulavīratantra, later Nātha and Kaula literature

Kubjikātantra denotes the scriptural corpus of the cult of the goddess Kubjikā ('the crooked/hunchbacked one'), the supreme Śakti and personification of kuṇḍalinī in the Paścimāmnāya (Western Transmission) of Kaula Shaivism. The root scripture is the Kubjikāmatatantra, which expounds the goddess, the deity Navātman, the maṇḍala, mantras, and yogic-ritual practice. Kubjikā is visualized as six-faced and twelve-armed, garlanded with skulls and serpents.

**History:** The Western Transmission is one of the four 'āmnāya' currents of Kaula Shaivism; the earliest evidence for the Kubjikā cult is from the tenth century, and its scriptures were shaped by both the Trika and Krama systems. The tradition flourished especially in Nepal, where its manuscripts are best preserved.

**Related works:** Kubjikāmatatantra, Ṣaṭsāhasrasaṃhitā, Trika and Krama tantras

The Lalleśvarīvākyāni ('Sayings of Lalleśvarī') are the terse mystical verses (vākhs) of the 14th-century Kashmiri yoginī Lal Dĕd, rooted in nondual Kashmir Shaivism. They express the inward quest for the Self/Śiva, the futility of empty ritual and ascetic extremism, the control of breath and mind, and direct experiential realization, in a vivid vernacular voice.

**History:** Composed in early Kashmiri (with Sanskritic and emerging Persian elements), the vākhs are among the earliest attested literary works in the Kashmiri language. Transmitted orally for centuries, they were first systematically recorded in writing in the early 20th century (George Grierson's Lallā-Vākyāni, 1920). Lal Dĕd is revered by both Hindus and Muslims in Kashmir.

**History:** Counted among the canonical Siddhānta āgamas of South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta, it survives mainly in manuscript and is used liturgically in temple practice. Like other āgamas it is anonymous and of uncertain date, transmitted through priestly lineages.

The Mṛgendrāgama (Mṛgendratantra) is a Śaiva Siddhānta scripture, treated as an upāgama / supplement of the Kāmikāgama. Its four pādas cover doctrine (vidyā), yoga, ritual (kriyā), and conduct (caryā); the Vidyāpāda in particular is a key statement of Siddhānta metaphysics—the categories of pati (Lord), paśu (bound soul), and pāśa (bonds).

**History:** It is one of the four āgamas relied upon by Śaiva Siddhānta that fall outside the standard list of twenty-eight. The tenth-century Kashmiri exegete Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha wrote an authoritative commentary (vṛtti) on it, and it was quoted and emulated by twelfth-century South Indian Siddhānta authors such as Aghoraśiva.

The Nareśvaraparīkṣā ('Examination of [the relation of] Man and the Lord') is a foundational philosophical treatise of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta by Sadyojyoti, the earliest systematizer of Siddhānta theology in Sanskrit. **History:** Sadyojyoti grounded his exposition in scriptures such as the Rauravāgama and Svāyambhuvasūtrasaṅgraha. The Nareśvaraparīkṣā received an important commentary (prakāśa) by the Kashmiri theologian Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha, and the work shaped the later, highly systematic Saiddhāntika exegesis of tenth-century Kashmir and twelfth-century South India.

**Related works:** Rauravāgama, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Nareśvaraparīkṣāprakāśa, Śaiva Siddhānta treatises

Two works grouped under the name Somānanda: the Parātriśikātātparyadīpikā, a commentary elucidating the 'inner purport' of the short but highly esteemed Parātriśikā (Parātrīśikā), the celebrated dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess on the supreme Power (Parā) drawn from the Rudrayāmala; and the Śāktavijñāna, a non-dual Śākta-Trika exposition of the knowledge (vijñāna) of Śakti. Together they treat the metaphysics of the highest goddess-energy, the emanation of the phonemic cosmos, and the recognition of consciousness as supreme reality.

The Parātriśikā itself attracted commentaries by Abhinavagupta (Vivaraṇa and Laghuvṛtti) and later Kashmirian and Śākta authors; attributions of further glosses such as this Dīpikā are sometimes uncertain.

**Related works:** Parātriśikā (Parātrīśikā), Rudrayāmala, Parātriśikāvivaraṇa of Abhinavagupta

An extraordinary 'Wish-fulfilling Tree', a multilingual crossword-like figure poem (carmen cancellatum) originally displayed on a large cloth, in which hidden inscribed texts ('intexts') are read out of a grid using roughly thirty languages. It is described as the largest carmen cancellatum known in world literature, a virtuoso devotional-poetic creation.

**History:** Composed in 17th-century Kashmir by Sāhib Kaul, a prolific and ambitious Śākta-Śaiva poet who also wrote the Devīnāmavilāsa, the Śyāmāpaddhati, and several ritual handbooks. Alexis Sanderson has argued Sāhib Kaul and his lineage introduced eastern-Indian Śākta elements into Kashmir and fused Advaita Vedānta with Pratyabhijñā. The Sanskrit text was edited for the first time by Jürgen Hanneder.

**Related works:** Devīnāmavilāsa, Śyāmāpaddhati

His commentary on the Vyomavyāpin/Vyomavyāpistava situates the hymn in the dualist Śaiva exegetical tradition.

**Related works:** Vyomavyāpin mantra, Niśvāsatattvasaṃhitā / Siddhānta Āgamas, works of Sadyojyotis

Engaging Advaita Vedānta, Sāṃkhya realism, and Buddhist positions, it establishes the doctrine that all reality is the self-recognition of Śiva.

**History:** Somānanda is regarded as the founder of the Pratyabhijñā school; his pupil Utpaladeva systematized and expanded the system, and it was later brought to its peak by Abhinavagupta. Utpaladeva wrote the (partly lost) Śivadṛṣṭivṛtti commentary.

The Spandasandoha is an extended exposition (sandoha) by Kṣemarāja concentrating on the opening verse(s) of the Spandakārikā. It elaborates the doctrine of spanda, the subtle creative 'vibration' or pulsation of divine consciousness (Śiva) that underlies all manifestation and cognition, and shows how recognition of this dynamic awareness yields liberation. It functions as a doctrinal and devotional gateway to the full Spanda system.

**History:** The mūla Spandakārikā is ascribed either to Vasugupta or to his pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa (9th c.); the record's attribution of the Spandasandoha to Kallaṭa is an error, as the Spandasandoha is the well-attested work of Kṣemarāja, disciple of Abhinavagupta. Kṣemarāja also wrote the fuller Spandanirṇaya covering the whole text; Kallaṭa's own contribution is the early Spandavṛtti.

**Related works:** Spandakārikā, Spandanirṇaya, Spandavṛtti (of Kallaṭa), Śivasūtra

The Śrītattvacintāmaṇi is a voluminous Śākta-tantric compendium in Sanskrit verse, organized into chapters (prakāśas), covering nearly the whole field of Tantra: initiation (dīkṣā), the subtle body and its cakras, kinds of mantra, tantric goddesses, and the worship of Tripurasundarī/Ṣoḍaśī and the Śrīcakra. **History:** Composed by Pūrṇānanda, a Bengali sādhaka, in 1577. The work runs to roughly twenty-six prakāśas; its sixth chapter (Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa) circulated independently and became internationally known through Arthur Avalon's translation 'The Serpent Power.' It is a major source for the systematized cakra-yoga of later Tantra.

**Related works:** Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (its 6th chapter), Tattvacintāmaṇi chapters 6-10/11-15/16-end

The Tantrāloka ('Light on the Tantras') is Abhinavagupta's monumental synthesis of Trika Śaivism, presented as an exposition of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra. Its first fourteen āhnikas lay the philosophical and soteriological foundations: the nature of Śiva-consciousness and its self-manifestation, the four 'means' (upāyas) to liberation (āṇava, śākta, śāmbhava, and the no-means anupāya), the categories of bondage and grace (śaktipāta), and the metaphysics of the universe as the expansion of consciousness.

**History:** Composed in early-11th-century Kashmir, the Tantrāloka comprises around 5,800 verses in 37 āhnikas and is the most authoritative systematic work of nondual Kashmiri Śaivism. It was illuminated by the indispensable Viveka commentary of Abhinavagupta's pupil Jayaratha (12th-13th c.).

**Related works:** Mālinīvijayottaratantra, Tantrasāra (Abhinavagupta's own digest), Tantrālokaviveka (Jayaratha), Tantrāloka chapters 15-38

He bridged Vedic orthodoxy and Tantric esotericism and advocated the right-hand (dakṣiṇa) path of Śrīvidyā. He also commented on the Lalitāsahasranāma, Saundaryalaharī, and Bhāvanopaniṣad.

**Related works:** Vāmakeśvarīmata/Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, Lalitāsahasranāma (with Bhāskararāya's Saubhāgyabhāskara), Setubandha (his comm. on Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava)

The Vātūlanāthasūtra is a short set of about thirteen terse aphorisms belonging to the Kashmiri Krama tradition. They expound the highest nondual realization—the 'great spontaneous leap' (mahāsāhasa-vṛtti) into Śiva-consciousness—and the supreme state of unmediated identity with the absolute, framed as revelation received from the Yoginīs.

The sūtras survive with the Sanskrit commentary (vṛtti) of Anantaśaktipāda, who frames them as a direct revelation from enlightened Yoginīs; neither sūtras nor commentary can be securely dated. The Pūrvabhāga (former/earlier part) of the Kāmikāgama, the first of the twenty-eight Siddhānta Śaivāgamas, a metrical scripture of about 12,000 verses in two parts. The Pūrvabhāga's seventy-five paṭalas treat the Śaiva ritual system in detail — daily obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika) and optional (kāmya) rites — together with temple architecture, consecration, the duties of priests and devotees, and elements of doctrine.

**History:** A primary scripture of South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta; traditionally regarded as revealed by Śiva. While portions may date to at least the 5th century, the currently published recensions were compiled and printed in the 19th century, and a critical edition project is ongoing.

**Related works:** Kāmikāgama (Uttarabhāga), Twenty-eight Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas

The Kāmikāgama is one of the principal scriptures (āgamas) of the South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta, a metrical work in two parts, the Pūrvabhāga and Uttarabhāga. The Uttarabhāga (roughly 98 chapters in anuṣṭubh meter) treats temple ritual, consecration, architecture, festivals, priestly duties, and the daily, occasional, and optional rites of Śaiva worship, with some doctrinal content. It is one of the most authoritative practical guides for Śaiva temple ritual in Tamil Nadu.

**History:** The Kāmika is counted among the twenty-eight mūla (root) Śaiva āgamas and is widely cited as a primary source of ritual authority in the Siddhānta tradition; like other āgamas its surviving form is the product of long transmission, and its printed Pūrva/Uttara recension was compiled and edited in the 19th century. It remains in active use by hereditary śivācārya temple priests.

**Related works:** Śaiva Āgamas (28 mūlāgamas), Kriyākramadyotikā

The Spandanirṇaya is Kṣemarāja's authoritative prose commentary on the Spandakārikā, the foundational verses of the Spanda ('vibration/pulsation') school of Kashmir Shaivism. It expounds the doctrine that the dynamic creative throb of consciousness (spanda) underlies all experience, and is regarded as the most complete and authoritative of the commentaries on the kārikās.

**History:** The root Spandakārikās are traditionally attributed to Vasugupta (with his disciple Kallaṭa, who wrote the Vṛtti and who is sometimes named as author); the title metadata's attribution to Kallaṭa reflects this debated authorship. Kṣemarāja, a direct disciple of Abhinavagupta, composed the Spandanirṇaya at the request of his disciple Śūra. The text is preserved in the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.

**Related works:** Spandakārikā, Spandavṛtti (Kallaṭa), Śivasūtra, Śivasūtravimarśinī

The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is a 700-verse dialogue in which the god Kṛṣṇa, as Arjuna's charioteer, counsels the despondent Pāṇḍava prince on the eve of the Kurukṣetra war. It synthesizes paths of action (karma), devotion (bhakti), and knowledge (jñāna) and presents a theology of God as the supreme reality, becoming the most influential single text of Hindu thought.

**History:** It forms chapters 23-40 of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata and is traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa, though scholars regard it as a composite work of multiple hands inserted into the epic. It has attracted major commentaries from Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, Madhva, Abhinavagupta, and others, and is central to every school of Vedānta.

**Related works:** Mahābhārata (Bhīṣmaparvan), Gītābhāṣya (Śaṅkara), Gītārthasaṃgraha (Abhinavagupta)

**Related works:** the 28 Śaiva Siddhāntāgamas (e.g., Kāmika, Kāraṇa, Ajita, Raurava)

The Śivadharmaśāstra is the foundational text of the Śivadharma corpus, a body of works prescribing the religious duties, devotional practices, and observances of the lay Śaiva community. The Śivadharmottara is the second principal text of the Śivadharma corpus, a sequel ('uttara') to the Śivadharmaśāstra. In roughly 1,750 verses across about twelve chapters it expounds dharma, worldly enjoyment (bhukti) and liberation (mukti), with emphasis on gift-giving, the merit of teaching and copying the Śivadharma itself, devotional discipline, and a notable chapter on yoga and meditation.

It is sometimes classed as an upāgama of the Śarvoktāgama within the Siddhānta scheme and survives in versions of twelve or thirteen chapters in different manuscript traditions.

**Related works:** Sarvajñānottaratantra, other works of Aghoraśivācārya (e.g. Mṛgendrapaddhati, Tattvaprakāśavṛtti)

A sub-commentary (dīpikā, 'lamp') by Aghoraśivācārya on the Vṛtti of Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha on the Mṛgendra(tantra/āgama), an authoritative scripture of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta. The Mṛgendravṛttidīpikā glosses the earlier Kashmirian Vṛtti of Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha and became a standard study aid for the Mṛgendra in the southern Siddhānta school.

**Related works:** Mṛgendrāgama / Mṛgendratantra, Mṛgendravṛtti (Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha), Kāmikāgama

Most of these Āgamas are lost or partially preserved in southern manuscript collections and ritual practice.

The slight variant in the title here ('nirṇaya' rather than 'nirūpaṇa') leaves some uncertainty about whether a distinct work is meant.

The title means 'joining/uniting with brahman' (brahma + sandhāna, 'fixing, conjunction, contemplation'). ## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 151 BCE – 1198 CE

**Posterior median:** 529 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Śaiva Siddhānta

**Genre:** agama (Śaiva scripture)

**Estimated date:** 1st millennium CE (undated; canonical Śaiva Siddhānta Āgama, formative c. 7th-10th c. CE)

A Siddhānta Śaiva Āgama (also classed as an Upāgama) styled a pratiṣṭhātantra, i.e. a scripture dealing primarily with the installation (pratiṣṭhā) and worship of liṅgas and other representations of Śaiva deities, temple ritual, and related kriyā. Its name ('moon-knowledge') links it to the lunar/calming aspect of Śiva worship.

**History:** Candrajñāna is enumerated among the 28 Śaiva Āgamas, traditionally proclaimed by the Tatpuruṣa face of Śiva and transmitted through Ananta/Bṛhaspati, and is said to have many Upāgamas. It survives chiefly in southern manuscript and ritual traditions and is cited in studies of Śaiva temple installation ritual.

**Related works:** the 28 Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas, Kāmikāgama, Kāraṇāgama

_Web summary confidence: medium_

The title means 'the essence (sāra) of the haṃsa', the haṃsa ('so'ham') being the spontaneous breath-mantra central to yoga and tantra, where Ha = exhalation and Sa = inhalation and the haṃsa is identified with the inner self/Śiva. **History:** Haṃsa speculation is widespread in tantric (e.g. Niruttara-type) and yogic literature and in Haṃsa/Haṃsopaniṣad material; a discrete text titled Haṃsasāra is not well documented in accessible sources, leaving its identification uncertain.

**Genre:** philosophical/devotional treatise

**Estimated date:** unknown (varies by work; Yaśovijaya's Jain Jñānasāra is 17th c. CE)

'The essence of knowledge.' Several distinct Sanskrit works bear this title. The best-known is the Jain Jñānasāra by Upādhyāya Yaśovijaya (1624-1688), a compact verse treatise on spiritual knowledge by a master of Navya-Nyāya; there are also Vedāntic/Advaita texts of the same name distilling Upaniṣadic teaching. Without further markers the intended work cannot be fixed.

**History:** Because 'Jñānasāra' is a common title across traditions, identification depends on context not given here. Yaśovijaya's Jñānasāra is among his roughly 100 works and is a standard Jain text; other Jñānasāras circulate in Vedānta and tantric anthologies.

**Related works:** Jñānasāra (Yaśovijaya), Adhyātmasāra (Yaśovijaya)

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Vedānta (minor/Sāmānya Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda)

**Genre:** Upaniṣad (philosophical/ritual scripture)

**Estimated date:** later Vedic/post-Vedic; commonly placed in the early centuries CE (one of the minor Upaniṣads)

A short Upaniṣad (about 23 verses) whose title means 'the fire-offering (agnihotra) into the fire of breath (prāṇa).' It internalizes the external Vedic agnihotra: eating is recast as an oblation to the digestive fire, the bodily prāṇas as the sacrificial fires, and the universal Self as dwelling within the body. It teaches that liberation can be attained by realizing the indwelling brahman even without external ritual or formal Sāṃkhya/Yoga.

**History:** It belongs to the corpus of minor (Sāmānya) Upaniṣads attached to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda and represents the transition from external Vedic sacrifice to internalized yogic/contemplative practice. It survives in standard Upaniṣad collections and editions.

**Related works:** minor Upaniṣads of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, Prāṇāgnihotra / agnihotra Vedic ritual literature

_Web summary confidence: high_

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 682 CE – 913 CE

**Posterior median:** 799 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Kashmir Śaivism (Trika / Bhairava stream)

**Genre:** tantra (yoga/meditation scripture)

**Estimated date:** c. 7th-8th c. CE (disputed)

A foundational Trika scripture of Kashmir Śaivism, framed as a dialogue between Bhairava (Śiva) and the Goddess, presenting 112 dhāraṇās (centering/meditation techniques) for attaining recognition of nondual consciousness. The methods range over breath awareness, concentration on bodily centres, sound and mantra, the senses, void, and direct nondual awareness, all aimed at realizing one's identity with Bhairava.

**History:** Said to be drawn from (a chapter of) the Rudrayāmala, it became a key text of the Trika and was commented on by Kṣemarāja and Śivopādhyāya; in the 20th century it was popularized in the West via Swami Lakshmanjoo and Paul Reps's 'Centering' (Zen Flesh, Zen Bones). Its exact date is uncertain, broadly placed in the 7th-9th centuries.

**Related works:** Rudrayāmalatantra, Trika/Kashmir Śaiva scriptures, Tantrāloka (Abhinavagupta)

_Web summary confidence: high_

The Umāsaṃhitā is one of the saṃhitās (books) of the Śivapurāṇa, the great Śaiva Purāṇa traditionally said to comprise seven saṃhitās and 24,000 verses. It expounds devotion (bhakti) to Śiva through meditation, prayer, and worship, and contains numerous narratives, including accounts of the goddess Umā/Pārvatī and Śaiva cosmology and eschatology.

**History:** As a saṃhitā of the Śivapurāṇa, it is anonymous and traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa; the Śivapurāṇa is a composite work compiled and recast over centuries. The number and arrangement of saṃhitās differ across recensions, and the Umāsaṃhitā is one of the standardly listed seven.

**Related works:** Śivapurāṇa

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_haharavatantraHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** hāhārāvatantra

**Description:** The Hāhārāvatantra (the Tantra of the Roaring Haa, Haa) teaches the worship of Kaula goddesses, especially forms of Kālī, with a very clear preference for Guhyakālī. Guhyakaalii is one of the most popular form of Kaalii in the Kathmandu Valley, although hardly known outside it. The main Tantra of Guhyakālī is the massive Mahākālasaṃhitā which may well have been redacted in Kathmandu Valley probably after the 14th century. It is likely that the Hāhārāvatantra is also of Nepalese as its preference for Guhyakālī suggests and absence of manuscripts or references to it outside the Valley. Another indication that this so is the presence in the text of the typical Nepalese corruption mahākarmārcana for mahaakramārcana denoting the Kaula liturgy for the worship of Kaula goddesses. This Tantra calls itself an atharvanasaṃhitā and so affiliates itself to the tradition of the Atharva Veda. This is probably because of its extensive treatment of magical rites, incantations and magical potions.

**Notes:** Revision 0: December 17, 2003

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

# Unknown: Kulānandādi

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kulanandadiHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulānandādi

**Description:** The manuscript called Kulānandādi contains short tracts and fragments of early Kaula works. The first is called Kulānanda covers the first seven folios. As it attributed to Matsyendranātha, it is important although short. It deals with aspects of Kaula Yoga, focused around the -piercing - (vedha) of spiritual energy through centres of the subtle body following from above and the piercing of Kuṇḍalinī upwards. The character and form of the exposition, which is in line with other Kaula tracts attributed to Matsyendranātha, supports the view that this is indeed an early Kaula work. The next 4 folios deal with the charateristics of a skull bowl (kapāla) which is said to be drawn from the Picumata (i.e. the Brahmayāmala) which is quite possible as this text does indeed deal with this topic. The rest of the manuscript contains prescriptions for Kaula ritual. The goddesses belong to the early period, including Kubjikā, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Bhagamālinī and others. Notably Tripurā is absent, although Kāmeśvarī, one of her precursors is not.

**Notes:** In the manuscript anusvāra and visarga occur together.

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**Estimated date:** c. 11th-13th c. CE (uncertain)

The title ('Kulānanda etc.') refers to the Kulānandatantra and associated short Kaula works. The Kulānandatantra is a brief Kaula scripture (about 60 verses) ascribed in its colophon to Matsyendra-pāda (Matsyendranātha), treating the cakras, granthis, and the piercing/ascent of the cakras in the Yoginī Kaula idiom.

**History:** The Kulānanda was published by P. C. Bagchi alongside the Kaulajñānanirṇaya of Matsyendranātha's school, from a Newari-script manuscript in the Darbar Library, Nepal. As with much of the Matsyendranātha corpus, authorship is traditional/ascriptive and dating is uncertain.

**Related works:** Kaulajñānanirṇaya, Akulavīratantra

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulasāra

**Description:** This manuscript is called Kulasāra, but is in fact a collection of fragment of three Kaula tracts. The first is Kaulsārasaṃgraha which, according to the colophons is a part of the Somabhujavalī. It begins with chapter 24 and extends up to to chapter 26. It is followed by the Kulaacāranirṇaya which extends from chapter 1 to 5. The third fragment is chapter eighteen of a work belonging to the śrīvidyā lineage of Subhagānandanātha. It deals with the funerary rites of a Kaula. The texts of which these are fragments in the format of a Tantra, outlining the principles of Kaula ritual and practice. They are typical Kaula work belonging to the latter period, that is, after the 13th century. Indeed such texts can be treated as an independent class of Kaula works of which the Kulārṇavatantra is one of the earliest.

**Notes:** Revision 0: December 17, 2013
