**Description:** āścaryayogamālā (also called Yogaratnāvalī or Yogaratnamālā) (the Rosary of Astonishing Yogas) by Nāgārjuna with a short commentary (laghuvṛtti) by Guṇākara who is a Jaina (śvetāmbara) scholar. This Nāgārjuna is famous as the author (or the namesake of various authors) of works on magic (ṣaṭkarma). A manuscript in the Asiatic Society in Bombay dates the composition of the work as 1240 CE. It was written, the text tells us, to serve people needs and delight them. It deals with standard matters of magic beginning with control of others (vaśīkaraṇa), then the checking of an enemies army (stambhana), killing of enemies (śatrumāraṇa), attraction of women (akarṣaṇa) and ways of attaining various magical powers (siddhi) through the preparation of potions, which the text describes in detail, and mantras.

An alchemical-medical work ('garland of wondrous applications/yogas') ascribed to the alchemist Nāgārjuna, offering rasa- and herbal recipes, mercurial and metallic preparations, and 'wondrous' efficacious formulae (yoga = prescription/combination). **History:** The name Nāgārjuna is a traditional, multiply-applied attribution attached to numerous alchemical and medical works (e.g. Rasaratnākara); such ascriptions are legendary and do not point to a single historical author, so the text's true date and authorship are uncertain.

The text is framed as a dialogue between Kākacaṇḍeśvarī (also called Kākacāmuṇḍā) who is equated with Kaṃkālī (the Skeleton) and Kālarātrī (Dark Night), both forms of Kālī. She is the consort (Umādevī) of the five headed Bhairava, who is probably with Svacchandabhairava, who is in some of his aspects a medicine god. They are seated on mount Kailāsa. After imploring him for the knowledge that leads to liberation, the god promising to do so, teaches the preparation of herbs for healing and magic most especially he focuses on the magical preparation of alchemical mercury making this an important unpublished work on Indian alchemy.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_GoraksayogasastraHK`

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** gorakṣayogaśāstram

**Author:** gorakṣanātha attributed to:

**Description:** Gorakṣayogaśāstram also called Mūlasāra the Essence of the Root this is a work on Yoga written in the manner of a stotra so that by reading and repeating it daily, one accfrues countless benefits. It opens with a summary of the contents of the subtle body, the vital channels, Sun, Moon and Fire, the Cakras and sacred Kaula sites, the Self that resides there, the 14 worlds, oceans, rivers all that is in the Egg of Brahmā is in the body. The Moon on the peak of the inner Mount Meru raisn down nectar throughout the body and so it goes on describing the activity and function of the inner contents of the body listed at the beginning. The treatise (śāstra) as its very name suggests is attributed to Gorakṣanātha, the founder of Haṭhayoga.

**Notes:** December 17, 2013

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 1046 CE – 1389 CE

**Posterior median:** 1217 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Śaiva (Nātha Sampradāya; Haṭha Yoga)

**Genre:** yoga treatise (śāstra)

**Estimated date:** c. 12th-15th c. CE (attribution traditional; core Gorakṣa material c. 1200 CE)

A yoga treatise of the Nātha tradition ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, teaching the methods of haṭha/laya yoga—posture, breath control (prāṇāyāma), the bandhas and mudrās, cakra meditation, and the raising of kuṇḍalinī—as the path to liberation. It belongs to the cluster of Gorakṣanātha-attributed yoga works (Gorakṣaśataka, Gorakṣasaṃhitā, etc.).

**History:** Authorship is traditional/ascriptive: a large body of Sanskrit yoga texts is attributed to Gorakṣanātha, founder-figure of the Nātha Sampradāya (c. 11th-12th c.), but many took their present form later and circulate in multiple recensions. The Gorakṣayogaśāstra is one such recension within this fluid corpus.

**Related works:** Gorakṣaśataka, Gorakṣasaṃhitā, Siddhasiddhāntapaddhati, Haṭhayogapradīpikā

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** tattvaratnāvalī

**Author:** vimalaśiva

**Description:** Tattvaratnāvalī by Vimalaśiva a South Indian Siddhāntin. This is a brief liturgical manual for the basic rites of Siddhānta śaivism. The first chapter deals with the regular daily rite (nitya) and the second with occasional rite (naimittika) performed on special festive occasions. The third chapter deals with the worship of the basic Navanābhamaṇḍala with nine sections, eight arranged around the central one each containing nine parts of the 81 parts (pada) of the Vyomavyāpin mantra which is the standard mantra of Siddhānta śaivism which begins with invocation of Sadāśiva as Vyomavyapin, that is, as -the one who pervades the sky-(written out fully on fl. 10)

**Notes:** Revision 0: December 17, 2013

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**Posterior median:** 1198 CE

_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Śaiva Siddhānta

**Genre:** philosophical treatise / paddhati (Śaiva ritual-doctrinal manual)

**Estimated date:** c. 11th-12th c. CE (uncertain)

A Saiddhāntika Śaiva work ('garland of jewels of the tattvas/principles') by Vimalaśiva, treating the categories (tattvas) and doctrine of the Śaiva Siddhānta and their ritual application. It belongs to the South-Asian Saiddhāntika exegetical and paddhati literature.

**History:** The text survives in a fragmentary, disordered palm-leaf manuscript (NAK 1-1697 / NGMPP B 26/16) and is little studied; Vimalaśiva is a Saiddhāntika author known chiefly from such manuscript witnesses, so dating remains tentative.

**Related works:** Somaśambhupaddhati, Tattvaprakāśa (Bhoja)

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** gorakṣaguṭikā

**Author:** gorakṣanātha

**Description:** The Goraksaguṭikā (the Magic Pill of Gorakṣa) is attributed to Gorakṣa (alias Gorakhnātha) the famous founder of Haṭha Yoga. The colophons state that it is part of the Kalpadrumavivekinii and that it is a commentary (bhyāsa) on Yoga. It is framed in the format of a Tantra as a dialogue between śiva and Gaurī. Although Gorakṣanātha was a yogi, as are his followers the Naatha Yogis today, and so should not be concerned with ritual practice, in actual fact the Nātha tradition has developed an extensive liturgy centered on the worship of its Gurus. This short tract contains a series of hymns (stotra) praising Gorakṣanātha and myths that narrate their origins.

**Notes:** Revision 0: Decemer 17, 2013

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 1068 CE – 1293 CE

**Posterior median:** 1182 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Śaiva (Nātha Sampradāya; Haṭha Yoga)

**Genre:** yoga treatise

**Estimated date:** c. 12th-15th c. CE (attribution traditional; related to the Gorakṣaśataka tradition)

A short Nātha yoga text ascribed to Gorakṣanātha, closely related to (and sometimes overlapping with) the Gorakṣaśataka recensions. It expounds the practice of haṭha/laya yoga—prāṇāyāma, bandhas, mudrās, cakra meditation, and kuṇḍalinī—as the means to liberation.

**History:** Like the other Gorakṣa-attributed works, its authorship is traditional and its text fluid across manuscripts and titles (Gorakṣaśataka, Gorakṣasaṃhitā, Gorakṣaguṭikā). It forms part of the foundational Nātha yoga corpus.

**Related works:** Gorakṣaśataka, Gorakṣasaṃhitā, Gorakṣayogaśāstra

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kālīkalpalatā

**Author:** vimarśānandanātha

**Description:** Kālīkalpalatā, also called Dakṣiṇakālīkalpalatā by Vimarśānandanātha is concerned with the ritual procedures for the worship of the goddess Dakṣiṇakālī and her consort Mahākāla. This form of Kālī is especially popular in Bengal. First presented by āgamakṛṣṇavāgīśa in his Bṛhattantrasāra written in the sixteenth century in Bengal, the Kālīkalpalatā post-dates it. The ritual procedure is described in sufficient detail to be able to perfom the ritual. It is divided into two sections (kusuma literally -flowers-) The first deals with the preliminary purifications, bathing and offering of libations. The second describes the puujaa itself.

**Notes:** Revision 0: December 17, 2013

**Provenance confidence:** high

**Estimated date:** late medieval / early modern (uncertain)

A Śākta ritual-compendium ('wish-granting creeper of Kālī') by Vimarśānandanātha, dealing with the worship of the goddess Kālī—her mantras, visualization, rites, and associated Kaula practices. It draws on and cites earlier tantric authorities (e.g. the Yāmala literature).

**History:** The work is cited in later scholarship as a source on Kālī worship and Śākta sacrificial practice; it belongs to the digest/paddhati literature of the Kālīkula. Its author Vimarśānandanātha and exact date are not firmly fixed.

**Related works:** Kālī Tantras, Yāmala tantras

# Unknown: Kulasāra

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kulasaraHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulasāra

**Description:** The manuscript is incomplete. It begins abruptly in the middle of chapter (paṭala) four and then continues from chapter eight to seventeen where it ends abruptly. The Kulasāra is quoted by non-dualist Kashmiri Shaiva authors and so preceeds the 11th century. It belongs to a genre of Kaula Tantras that are focused on the attainment of the direct experience of essential metaphysical principles and yogic powers through the practice of Yoga and insight. Through knowledge of these principles the Kaula Yogi attains liberation in this life (jñānāvabhāsena jīvanmuktye vyavasthitaḥ fl. 33b) and numerous yogic powers. The text focuses also on the worship of Bhairava and Devī and the host of Yoginīs. The first chapters are concerned with the four principles commonly mentioned in Kaula works, namely, Piṇḍa, Pada, ṛūpa and Rūpātīta. Unfortunately, here the manuscript is incomplete. Chapter nine deals with the attainment of the pervasion of transcendental śiva by the abandonment of śakti (9). The following chapter teaches the attainment of the supreme reality which is the Inexplicable free of phenomenal qualities, immobile and pervasive like the sky by merger with the space contained in the jar of the psycho-physical body (10). The next chapter deals with transcendent Akula and immanent Kula along with Kaula which is the union of the two (11). Chapter twelve describes the ascent through the centres of the body from the feet to the head. Corresponding to the spheres of the gross elements, they are the abodes of numerous types of Yoginīs the text describes and the damage they can do. The Yogi should know them and by his devotion to the deity, fire and the guru and practice of Yoga be protected from them. Those who are immoral are consummed by them. The chapter ends with a series of visualizations designed to protect the body of the Yogi (12). The next chapter continues with similar concerns for protection and the overcoming of disease and death by the use of Bhairava Mantra and visualization of his form which appears to be that of Svacchandabhairava and accompanying forms and their consorts (13). The next chapter discusses non-duality in the sense of the absence of pure and impure with regards to food and drink and the defects of those who do not follow this path. It goes on to talk about freedom from dualistic thought constructs and the purification of the mind and purification of the sacrificial substances that takes place in this way. It is applied to the sacrificial meat and then wine (14). Chapter fifteen deals with the observance (caryā) of the Kaula adept (vīra). He should travel to the inner Kaula sacred sites (pīṭha, kṣetra) in the body following the vital breath rather than the outer ones. There he plays with the Yoginīs and worships them and does so externally also with a pure mind. The manner the pilgrimage is to be performed externally is described next.The last chapter deals with the Three Jewels of Shiva, Shakti and the Self, their attainment and experience.

**Notes:** Revision 0: December 17, 2013

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 188 CE – 1297 CE

**Posterior median:** 734 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Śaiva-Śākta (Kaula / early Trika)

**Genre:** tantra

**Estimated date:** c. 8th-10th c. CE (early Kaula stratum; uncertain)

An early Kaula Śaiva scripture (a second record of the same title as M00285) transmitting Kaula doctrine, the worship of Śiva-Śakti, kuṇḍalinī/cakra schemes, mantra, and transgressive Kaula ritual. It is part of the formative Kaula scriptural corpus drawn on by later Trika/Kaula exegetes.

**History:** Preserved in early Nepalese manuscripts, the Kulasāra is among the old Kaula sources studied in connection with Alexis Sanderson's work on the early Śaiva-Śākta corpus; it is anonymous and hard to date precisely. This entry duplicates the title of work M00285.

**Related works:** Kaula tantras, Kulārṇavatantra, Kulasāra (M00285)

# Vimalaśiva: Vimalāvatītantra

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_vimalavatiitantraHK`

**Author:** Vimalaśiva

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** vimalāvatītantra

**Author:** vimalaśiva

**Description:** This is a work on Siddhānta ritual written by Vimalaśiva who lived in the thirteenth century. He declares with pride that he had taken the vow of residing all his life in Benares (kāśīvāsa). The first chapter deals with the accomplishment and fruits of worship (pūjāsiddhi). Chapter two deals with the procedure for making the sacrificial; fire (vahnikārya) and three the offerings to it (homa). Four deals with the seasonal offering to the deity of a sacred thread (pavitra) and the next with the offering of garlands (dāmana). The fifth deals with the rites of initiation. The text continues to elaborate on the details concerning initiation. It includes several interesting inner purificatory practices linked with the movement of the vital breath and the movement of Kuṇḍalinī. The rules of right conduct for initiate of various kinds are ennumerated and other matters taught concerning his duties and those of Shaivites in general both as householders and renouncers. Various initiatory rites are described for different types and levels of initiands.

**Notes:** Revision 0: December 17, 2013

**Publication country:** India

**Provenance confidence:** high

## Date estimate ([Statistical Model](https://dharmamitra.github.io/sanskrit-dating/sanskrit_chronology_interactive.html))

**95% credible interval:** 309 CE – 1389 CE

**Posterior median:** 845 CE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu, Śaiva (Siddhānta/Āgama)

**Genre:** tantra (āgama)

**Estimated date:** uncertain (medieval Śaiva)

A Śaiva tantra/āgama; the title is connected with the 'Vimala' āgamic line (Vimalāgama is counted among the twenty-eight Siddhāntāgamas of the Śaiva canon proclaimed by the Tatpuruṣa face of Śiva). As a Siddhānta āgama it would treat doctrine, ritual worship, consecration, and yoga.

**History:** The text is obscure and poorly documented; the project's attribution to Vimalaśiva is uncertain, and the title may relate to the Vimalāgama tradition rather than to a securely identified single work. No critical edition or firm dating is available.

**Related works:** Vimalāgama, Śaiva Siddhāntāgamas

One of the twenty minor 'Yoga Upaniṣads', cast as a teaching of the sage Dattātreya to Sāṃkṛti. It expounds an eight-limbed (aṣṭāṅga) yoga, the nāḍīs and cakras of the subtle body, prāṇāyāma, purificatory practices and meditation aimed at realizing the non-dual Self (Brahman/Ātman).

**History:** It is a sectarian Yoga Upaniṣad usually affiliated to the Sāmaveda and absorbed into late anthologies of the 108 Upaniṣads; its precise authorship and date are unknown, and scholars debate whether it predates or postdates Patañjali's Yogasūtra. It is preserved within the South Indian Muktikā canon and printed in collections of the minor Upaniṣads.

**Related works:** Yoga Upaniṣads (collection), Muktikā Upaniṣad canon, Patañjali Yogasūtra, Śāṇḍilya Upaniṣad

A minor Yoga Upaniṣad attached to the Śukla Yajurveda in which a brāhmaṇa named Triśikhin questions the sun-deity. It teaches non-dualist Vedānta through yoga, treating the unity of Brahman, Ātman and the world, and presenting an eight-limbed yoga with prāṇāyāma, āsana and meditative absorption as the means to liberating self-knowledge.

**History:** It belongs to the corpus of twenty Yoga Upaniṣads incorporated into the late Muktikā canon; its authorship is unknown and its dating is contested, with much of its content overlapping later haṭha-yoga literature. It survives in South Indian Upaniṣad anthologies and printed editions of the minor Upaniṣads.

A minor Yoga Upaniṣad of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda in five chapters (c. 251 verses), framed as a dialogue between Viṣṇu as the boar-avatāra Varāha and the sage Ṛbhu. It surveys the tattvas (lists of 24, 36 and 96), the path to liberation, realization of the Self, jīvanmukti, and incorporates tantric and yogic material on cakras, nāḍīs, mantra, laya and haṭha yoga.

**History:** A demonstrably late Upaniṣad, it is absent from the 17th-c. Dārā Shikoh and early-19th-c. Colebrooke anthologies, and its authorship and source are uncertain. It is preserved in the South Indian Muktikā canon and printed among the thirty minor Upaniṣads.

**Related works:** Yoga Upaniṣads (collection), Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, Muktikā Upaniṣad canon

**History:** An obscure text known mainly through manuscript catalogues (Muktabodha M00328); independent scholarship securely identifying its author, date and precise contents is lacking, so the affiliation is inferred chiefly from the title.

**Related works:** Yogavāsiṣṭha (whole), Laghu-Yogavāsiṣṭha, Rāmāyaṇa

The Yogavāsiṣṭha is a vast Advaitic verse dialogue (c. 23,000-32,000 verses) framed as the sage Vasiṣṭha instructing the young Rāma on the unreality of the phenomenal world, the nature of mind and consciousness, liberation while living (jīvanmukti), and the path of knowledge, illustrated by elaborate philosophical fables. The Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī became the most widely printed commentary, notably in the Nirṇaya-sāgara Press edition of Wāsudeva Laxman Śāstrī Paṇaśīkar.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** sādhanamālā Vol. 1

**Author:** benoytosh bhattacharya

**Description:** This text is a collection of sādhanas, that is, procedures for the worship of Buddhist Tantric deities especially those of the Anuttarayoga Tantras. A description of the deity, its form and colour, vehicle etc along with its related visualization is supplied in each sādhana together with that deitys Mantra and its applications in worship and yogic practice. They are composed by a large range of Buddhist teachers many of eminence. The earliest is the Siddha Saraha who is dated to around 630 CE. Along with him are a number of other great Buddhist Siddhas, such as Nāgārjuna, Kukkuripa, Indrabhūti, Kṛṣṇapāda, śabara and others who belonged to the 7th and 8th century. The last contributors belong to the 12th century which gives us a lower limit for the date of the collection.

The Sādhanamālā ('garland of sādhanas') is a large anthology of several hundred Buddhist tantric sādhanas — visualization and ritual-worship texts for evoking Vajrayāna deities such as Avalokiteśvara, Tārā, Mañjuśrī, Hevajra, and many forms of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. It is a primary source for Buddhist iconography and tantric liturgy. Volume 1 contains the first portion of the collected sādhanas.

**History:** Compiled from numerous authors over centuries, the anthology was critically edited by Benoytosh Bhattacharyya from eight manuscripts and published in the Gaekwad's Oriental Series (Vol. I, 1925). It is foundational to the modern study of Buddhist tantric art and ritual.

**Related works:** Sādhanamālā, Vol. 2, Niṣpannayogāvalī, Buddhist Iconography (Bhattacharyya)

The Śrīkarabhāṣya is a commentary on the Brahmasūtras (Vedāntasūtras) of Bādarāyaṇa expounding the Vīraśaiva theological standpoint, often termed Śakti-Viśiṣṭādvaita or Vīraśaiva-Viśiṣṭādvaita. **History:** Its author Śrīpati Paṇḍitācārya styled himself a Vīraśaiva ascetic; the work is the principal Vedāntic foundation for Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) philosophy. It was discussed at length by historians of Indian philosophy such as S. N. Dasgupta.

**Related works:** Brahmasūtra (Bādarāyaṇa), Śrībhāṣya (Rāmānuja), Vīraśaiva āgama literature

The Śivasūtra is the foundational aphoristic scripture of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, traditionally revealed to the sage Vasugupta, setting out the nature of universal Consciousness (Caitanya) as the Self, the means (upāyas) to liberation, and the powers of the realized yogin in three sections. **History:** Tradition holds that Vasugupta found the sūtras inscribed on a rock (Mahādeva mountain) by Śiva's grace. Kṣemarāja, a disciple of Abhinavagupta, produced the Vimarśinī, the standard commentary that frames the Śivasūtra within Trika-Pratyabhijñā doctrine.

**Related works:** Śivasūtra (Vasugupta), Spandakārikā, Spandanirṇaya (Kṣemarāja), Śivasūtravārttika

The Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya ('the heart of recognition') is Kṣemarāja's concise primer of the Pratyabhijñā philosophy, consisting of twenty short sūtras with his own auto-commentary. It distills the doctrine that the entire universe is the free self-manifestation of one absolute Consciousness (Citi/Śiva), and that liberation is the recognition (pratyabhijñā) of one's true nature as that Consciousness.

**History:** Written by Kṣemarāja as an accessible introduction to the more technical Pratyabhijñā works of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta; it remains the most popular entry-point text to non-dual Kashmir Śaivism and has been widely translated (e.g. by Jaideva Singh).

**Related works:** Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā (Utpaladeva), Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (Abhinavagupta), Śivasūtravimarśinī (Kṣemarāja)

The Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha ('shorter Yogavāsiṣṭha') is a condensed recension of the large Yogavāsiṣṭha, retaining its Advaitic teaching on the unreality of the world, the mind, and liberation-in-life through the Vasiṣṭha-Rāma dialogue, in a more manageable compass. This edition adds the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā commentary.

The Spandakārikā ('verses on vibration') is the root text of the Spanda branch of Kashmir Śaivism, teaching that ultimate reality is a dynamic, throbbing Consciousness (spanda) — the creative pulsation of Śiva — and that recognizing this vibration in all states of experience is the means to liberation. **History:** The kārikās are traditionally attributed either to Vasugupta or to his pupil Kallaṭa Bhaṭṭa, and are closely linked to the Śivasūtra. Several commentaries exist (Kallaṭa's Vṛtti, Rāmakaṇṭha's Vivṛti, and Kṣemarāja's Spandanirṇaya); Rāmakaṇṭha's Vivṛti is one of the earliest.

**Related works:** Śivasūtra (Vasugupta), Spandanirṇaya (Kṣemarāja), Spandasandoha (Kṣemarāja)

The Aniruddhasaṃhitā is a Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava āgama of thirty-four chapters (c. 1800 granthas) prescribing temple ritual: modes of worship, initiation (dīkṣā), expiations (prāyaścitta), image-making and installation, and especially the annual temple festival cycle, to which it gives unusual attention, along with topics such as royal duty (rājadharma) and town planning.

**History:** One of the many (200+) Pāñcarātra saṃhitās, most preserved only in manuscript; named after Aniruddha, one of the vyūha (emanation) forms of Viṣṇu. It is a source for South Indian Vaiṣṇava temple liturgy.

**Related works:** Pāñcarātra Saṃhitā literature (e.g. Pādma, Pārameśvara, Sāttvata, Jayākhya saṃhitās), Viśvaksena Saṃhitā

The Pārānandasūtra is an aphoristic Tantric work expounding Kuladharma — described as the 'cream of the Vedas' — and teaching that the Supreme Being is one, while accommodating seven sectarian deities (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, Śakti, Bhairava). It treats the three paths of sādhana (Dakṣiṇa, Vāma, Uttara mārga) and stresses initiation (dīkṣā) from a qualified, ideally jīvanmukta, guru.

**History:** Regarded as one of the earlier extant Tantric sūtra texts (c. 900 CE), it is cited in surveys of Hindu Tantric/Śākta literature as an important witness to Kaula doctrine and its relation to Vedic authority.

**Related works:** Kaula Tantric literature, Kulārṇavatantra

The Nāṭyaśāstra is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on the performing arts, encyclopedically covering drama (nāṭya), dance, music, stagecraft, gesture, costume, the structure of plays, and above all the theory of aesthetic experience (rasa and bhāva). Volume 1 contains the opening chapters, including the mythic origin of theatre, the construction of the playhouse, and the foundational rasa/bhāva doctrine.

**History:** Ascribed to the legendary sage Bharata, it is in fact a composite work compiled over centuries. It is the single most influential text on Indian aesthetics, drama, and music, and generated a long commentarial tradition culminating in Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabhāratī.

**Related works:** Abhinavabhāratī (Abhinavagupta's commentary), Daśarūpaka (Dhanañjaya), Saṅgītaratnākara

The Guhyasamājatantra ('tantra of the secret assembly/union') is one of the most important Buddhist Anuttarayoga (father) tantras, centered on the deity Akṣobhya/Guhyasamāja and the maṇḍala of the Five Buddhas. It systematizes the generation and completion stages of tantric yoga, deity visualization, mantra, and subtle-body practices, and is famous for its deliberately transgressive, antinomian symbolic language.

**History:** Considered the foundational text of its class, it is traditionally placed at the head of the Anuttarayoga corpus. It generated two major exegetical lineages — the Ārya (Nāgārjuna/Āryadeva attribution) and the Jñānapāda schools — and is central to later Indo-Tibetan Vajrayāna.

**Related works:** Pradīpoddyotana (Candrakīrti's commentary), Pañcakrama (attributed Nāgārjuna), Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha

**History:** Often cited as the earliest surviving Indian Buddhist tantra, it is an anonymous, composite text whose core may be sixth-century with substantial later additions; the whole is frequently dated to the later eighth century. Its 'historical' chapter has been mined (controversially) by historians for the chronology of the Guptas and other dynasties. The standard edition is the three-part Trivandrum Sanskrit Series text edited by T. Ganapati Sastri (1920-1925).

**History:** Composed by Kṣemarāja, the foremost disciple of Abhinavagupta (early 11th c.), author of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, Spandanirṇaya, and Śivasūtravimarśinī. The Parāprāveśikā is among his shorter introductory works on Pratyabhijñā doctrine.

**Related works:** Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya, Spandanirṇaya, works of Abhinavagupta

The foundational text of the Nyāya school, comprising about 528 aphorisms (sūtras) in five books. The oldest of the four Vedas and the foundational text of Indian religion: a collection of 1,028 hymns (sūktas) in 10 maṇḍalas, composed in archaic Vedic Sanskrit. The hymns invoke and praise deities such as Agni, Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, and Uṣas, and contain cosmogonic, ritual, and speculative poetry.

A concise introductory manual of the syncretic Navya-Nyāya/Vaiśeṣika system, expounding the seven categories (padārthas) of Vaiśeṣika ontology together with Nyāya epistemology, including the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇas) and especially the theory of inference (anumāna). **History:** Annambhaṭṭa, a scholar associated with Banaras and originally from Andhra, composed both the root text and his own commentary, the Tarkasaṃgraha-dīpikā. The work became one of the most widely used elementary textbooks of Indian logic, attracting numerous later commentaries and remaining standard in traditional pāṭhaśālā education to this day.

**Related works:** Tarkasaṃgraha-dīpikā, Tarkabhāṣā, Nyāyasūtra, Vaiśeṣikasūtra

A Vaiṣṇava Mahāpurāṇa framed as a dialogue between Viṣṇu and his eagle mount Garuḍa. Its first, encyclopedic part (Pūrva-khaṇḍa / Ācāra-kāṇḍa) covers cosmology, worship, ethics, gemmology, medicine (Āyurveda) and astrology, while its celebrated later portion, the Preta-kāṇḍa, deals with death, the fate of the soul, karmic punishments in the hells, and the rites for the departed (śrāddha).

**History:** One of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, the text is composite and grew over centuries, with the eschatological Preta-kāṇḍa becoming its best-known section, traditionally recited at funerals. Its dating is disputed, with scholars placing the layered core in the early medieval period.

The fourth Veda, a collection of hymns, spells, charms and incantations addressing everyday life: healing of diseases, protection from demons and rivals, love and marriage, prosperity, royal consecration, and also speculative cosmological and philosophical hymns. Jonarāja's Dvitīyā Rājataraṅginī is a verse chronicle of the kings of Kashmir that continues Kalhaṇa's original Rājataraṅginī, picking up the narrative around 1148/1150 CE and carrying it down to the reign of his patron Sultan Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (mid-15th c.). It vividly records the decline of the Hindu dynasties and the rise of Muslim rule and conversion in Kashmir.

**History:** Jonarāja died before completing the chronicle; his pupil Śrīvara continued it as the Tṛtīyā Rājataraṅginī. An interpolated recension known as Pseudo-Jonarāja contains additional verses. The project metadata's date hint (1100-1200) conflates Jonarāja with Kalhaṇa and is incorrect; Jonarāja belongs to the 15th century.

**Related works:** Rājataraṅginī (Kalhaṇa), Tṛtīyā Rājataraṅginī (Śrīvara), Jaina-Rājataraṅginī

An enormous Sanskrit collection of tales, fables, romances and legends ('Ocean of the Streams of Story'), arranged in 124 chapters within a frame narrative centering on Naravāhanadatta. It interweaves popular folklore, vidyādhara fantasy, and didactic and erotic narratives into a vast embedded story-within-story structure.

**History:** Composed by the Kashmiri Brahmin poet Somadeva for the entertainment of Queen Sūryavatī, wife of King Anantadeva of Kashmir. It is a Sanskrit recension of the lost Bṛhatkathā of Guṇāḍhya (originally in Paiśācī), parallel to Kṣemendra's Bṛhatkathāmañjarī, and is a major source for comparative folklore and the migration of tale-motifs.

The ninth and final chapter of Vasubandhu's prose auto-commentary on the Abhidharmakośa, known as the Pudgalaviniścaya ('Determination concerning the Person') or Ātmavādapratiṣedha ('Refutation of the Doctrine of Self'). It argues that liberation is impossible without abandoning belief in a self, and systematically refutes self/soul theories: chiefly the pudgala doctrine of the Vātsīputrīya/Sāṃmitīya Buddhists, and also the ātman of the Brahmanical Vaiśeṣikas.

**History:** Unlike the preceding eight chapters, this section is composed entirely in prose without root kārikās and is generally regarded as an independent treatise appended to the Kośa. It is a landmark statement of the Buddhist no-self (anātman) doctrine and a key source for understanding inter-Buddhist controversy on personhood.

A treatise on dharma, also styled the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra, largely a collection of older legal aphorisms set within a Vaiṣṇava devotional frame in which the god Viṣṇu instructs the Earth-goddess. Markers such as the centrality of written documents, mention of satī, and Kashmiri Vaiṣṇava iconographic correlations point to composition in the early medieval period, making it among the latest works of the Dharmaśāstra tradition.

A versified commentary (vārttika) on the Śivasūtra of Vasugupta, the foundational aphoristic scripture of the non-dual Trika system of Kashmir Shaivism that expounds the nature of bondage and the yogic means to liberation. One of the principal Mahāpurāṇas and a foundational text of Vaiṣṇavism, structured as the teaching of the sage Parāśara to his pupil Maitreya. It treats cosmogony, cosmic geography, the genealogies of gods and kings, the four yugas and manvantaras, the duties of caste and life-stage, and devotion to Viṣṇu, including an account of Kṛṣṇa's life.

A foundational verse treatise of Advaita Vedānta in four chapters (prakaraṇas): the first comments on the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad and the three states of consciousness plus turīya; the later chapters (Vaitathya, Advaita, Alātaśānti) argue for the unreality of the phenomenal world, the doctrine of non-origination (ajātivāda), and non-duality, drawing on dialectical methods with notable parallels to Buddhist (Madhyamaka/Yogācāra) thought.

**History:** Attributed to Gauḍapāda, traditionally the teacher of Śaṅkara's teacher Govinda. ## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu / secular-scientific (Āyurveda)

**Genre:** medical treatise (saṃhitā)

**Estimated date:** core c. 2nd c. BCE-2nd c. CE, with redaction by Caraka and later additions by Dṛḍhabala (c. 4th-5th c. CE); composite

One of the two foundational classics of Āyurveda, focused chiefly on internal medicine (kāyacikitsā). It treats physiology, the three doṣas, diagnosis, pathology, therapeutics, pharmacology, diet, ethics of the physician, and medical methodology, organized into eight sections (sthānas) and structured around the teaching lineage of Ātreya-Agniveśa.

**History:** Traditionally the Agniveśatantra composed by Agniveśa (pupil of Ātreya Punarvasu), redacted by Caraka, with the lost portions later restored by Dṛḍhabala. It is a layered text foundational to classical Indian medicine and was commented upon by Cakrapāṇidatta among others; it was transmitted in Arabic and influenced wider medical traditions.

**Related works:** Suśrutasaṃhitā, Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya (Vāgbhaṭa), Agniveśatantra

_Web summary confidence: high_

**95% credible interval:** 704 BCE – 470 BCE

**Posterior median:** 587 BCE

## Web Summary
_🤖 AI-generated overview — not human-verified; may contain inaccuracies._

**Tradition:** Hindu (Vedic / Vedānta)

**Genre:** Upaniṣad (Vedic philosophical text)

**Estimated date:** c. 8th-6th c. BCE (one of the oldest, pre-Buddhist Upaniṣads)

One of the oldest and largest principal Upaniṣads, belonging to the Sāmaveda and embedded in the Chāndogya Brāhmaṇa. In eight chapters it moves from the symbolism of the udgītha and the syllable Oṃ to profound metaphysical teachings, including the doctrine of Brahman as the Self, the dialogue of Śvetaketu and the great saying 'tat tvam asi' ('that thou art'), and Sanatkumāra's instruction on bhūman.

**History:** A foundational source for Vedānta, it is among the most frequently cited Upaniṣads in the Brahmasūtra and the commentaries of Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja and others. Its prose dialogues are key documents of early Indian philosophical and religious thought.

**Related works:** Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad, Sāmaveda, Brahmasūtra

_Web summary confidence: high_
